speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Prime Minister. speechtext:
May I
direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs? Is the Secretary of State for External Affairs in a position to confirm reports that in Wednesday's riots in Saigon, Indo-China, no Canadians were injured, including members of the Canadian mission? May I ask him at the same time what steps are being taken by the Canadian government in the light of the outbreak of disorder there and the damage that was done to property of Canadians?

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: VIET NAM TRUCE COMMISSION- RIOTS IN SAIGON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is true that when the riot took place at Saigon last Wednesday, a great deal of damage was done to the property, personal and official, of the international commission in Viet Nam, but no member of the Canadian side of the commission was affected either personally or through loss of property. We are all, of course, grateful for that fact.
Immediately on receipt of the news of these riots we sent a telegram to our representative on the commission asking him to associate himself with the other members of the commission in protesting to the Viet Nam authorities. We also expressed the hope that the ringleaders of the riot could be apprehended, that they would be suitably punished and that adequate steps would be taken by the authorities concerned to prevent the recurrence of such deplorable events. The Indian government, of course, supplied the chairman of the commission and I also understand that the Indian government has made an approach to the co-chairmen of last year's Geneva conference, from which the armistice commission derives its authority through the agreement concluded then, to take the question of these riots under advisement at Geneva where they happen to be now.

I should like to ask the minister what revenue is derived by the department from the services given by the airports to the various airlines?

Mr. Chairman, I have not the information directly related to individual air lines. I do not know whether the hon. member would like to know the total revenue. I might say that I have the figures here in

great detail and if the hon. member would perhaps be a little more specific as to the information he would like to have, I shall try to satisfy his request for information.
I should like to know the total revenue.
It is not difficult to give the total, Mr. Chairman. In 1953-54, the latest figures available, the total revenue was $5,164,596.

In that connection, might I ask this question. If additional aids to safety are provided, perhaps an additional charge would be made, and would the minister then say my suggestions of yesterday were as irresponsible as he implied last night.

I am sorry if the hon. member thought that my remarks last night suggested any irresponsibility on his part. No such thought was in my mind. If anything I said gave him that impression or gave anyone else that impression, I should like to correct it. There is, I think, no very real connection between the cost of radio aids and the landing fees that are charged to the air lines.
I might say to the committee that I know that some of the air lines think the landing fees are too high already, but that the officials of my department seem to think that some upward revision of them might be made. I would merely say that I do not believe we should consider the installation of radio aids in relation to landing fees. I think we have got to progress in a rational way in our installation of radio aids. I think we already have a very modern installation, and I hope that nothing that was said last night would give the impression that the I.L.S. system is not an effective means of permitting aircraft to make use of airports in bad weather, or that G.C.A. had such tremendous advantages over I.L.S. that we should have installed G.C.A. long ago. I do not think there is any important body of opinion in the aviation industry that would contend that G.C.A. had such a marked superiority over I.L.S. As I said last night, the commercial operators have favoured I.L.S. rather than G.C.A.
As I pointed out last night, the conditions at Gander are a little different. I am not talking about the geographical conditions or climatic conditions, I am talking about the kind of use that Gander has which makes G.C.A. more important there than anywhere else. I would not for a moment wish the committee to have the impression that because we have I.L.S. we are behind the times in our major airports.

notice there is a new provision of $112,000 for cleaning the airports at Dorval and Malton.

Will the minister give us a few details as to whether this applies only to airport buildings or whether it is more extensive?

The explanation of this item of $112,000 is that it represents the amount that it is proposed to pay under contracts with private operators for the performance of cleaning services both at Malton and Dorval airports in order to obtain more satisfactory and more economical performance of this type of work. This has been done previously by departmental employees, and the estimated cost of so doing it was $143,000, so that the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace will appreciate that there has been a quite substantial saving in consequence of this change of method in dealing with the cleaning at these two particular airports. I should say that the breakdown is $72,000 at Dorval and $40,000 at Malton.
Does that apply just to the public buildings at the various airports?
Yes.

In
other words, for these two public buildings used by passengers for emplaning and deplaning we are spending a total of $112,000 to keep them clean?

My hon. friend will understand that includes not only the public space in those buildings, but also includes the other space used for office purposes, for meteorological services, and the like. It is not just the public space in the buildings, as my hon. friend suggests.

would say, first, that I think it has been generally accepted and generally known by those who use the airports, not only at Malton and Dorval but at many other points across Canada, that the conditions of those airports, so far as cleanliness is concerned, are not all that could be desired.
One can easily understand that with the large numbers of people going through these buildings each day, and practically each hour of the day, it could not be expected that the buildings would be kept as neat as a pin, or without the occasional piece of paper on the floor. But my own personal experience, and that of many others who have spoken to me and who have gone through these buildings, has been that their state of cleanliness was quite unsatisfactory, such as to indicate that sufficient attention had not been paid to this particular problem.
Therefore I think we can express satisfaction that the government has realized the importance of the problem and is taking

certain steps, or perhaps has taken them, to see that corrective measures are brought about. However, I do question the amount being spent under these two contracts. I do not think it is a defence or an explanation simply to say that previously, when it was done by the government, the cost was higher.
Defence against what?

Against the charge that, at a figure of $112,000, we are still paying too much for the cleaning of these two buildings. The minister has explained that his estimate of its being done by the government would be $143,000, and that his being able to get it done under contract for $112,000 would be a satisfactory solution. I would point out to him however that, even if we allow the going rate for people doing this kind of work, a rate of somewhere in the neighbourhood of $200 a month which, according to my experience, is somewhat more than one would expect, we have here an amount of money sufficient to employ a staff of about 50 people.
Anyone who has been through the terminals at Malton or Dorval must realize that if we were to split the staff between the two of them, thus having 25 at each point, such staff would be absurdly large. It is very difficult to see what on earth they could find to do. I suggest to the minister that he might again look at this particular contract, not in the light of the previous inefficient government operation, but in the light of the actual requirements for the jobs. Let me say, however, that it is urgent and necessary that more attention be paid to the state of cleanliness of our airports and the proper undertaking of this important job.

Mr. Chairman, I would not like these rather general statements of the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace to pass unchallenged. I would like to talk about Malton and Dorval in a moment, but I would like to tell hon. members of this committee that I have visited quite a number of airports in the last year, and I do not share the opinion that the hon. gentleman has just expressed as to the state of cleanliness. There are a great many of our terminal buildings of which the Canadian people can very properly be proud. There are a number of buildings in various parts of the country which serve as models of what airports should be in the kind of places in which they are located.
I have seen airports elsewhere in Europe and in the United States, and all I can say is that no matter where one goes, particularly

Supply-Transport
on this side of the border, there are airports that are a great credit to the nation and others that are not so. Why? Because traffic varies and sometimes it happens, as it has happened at Malton and Dorval, that the traffic has grown at such a rapid rate that the facilities have been left behind. That applies in Canada just as it applies in the United States.
My hon. friend knows that at Dorval we have two terminal buildings. We have what is known as the international terminal which is-let us admit quite candidly-a relic of war days. We have the domestic building which is of an earlier date, and which is admittedly inadequate. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, when you have buildings that were built for the volume of traffic of a number of years ago, that it is not surprising that they are not in the best of condition at this time. The volume of traffic has grown unbelievably rapidly and the present facilities are overtaxed. No matter whether the cleaning of the buildings be done by the department itself, or by outside contractors, because of the intensity of the use I am afraid it is impossible to avoid completely criticisms of uncleanliness from time to time during the day. It seems to me to be practically unavoidable. Much the same situation, as a good many hon. members know, exists at Malton. The airport facilities there are very definitely overtaxed. Before I became Minister of Transport I had the misfortune to have to spend four hours in the terminal building at Toronto because it was necessary to repair one of the engines of the plane. During the four hours I had a very excellent opportunity of finding out how narrow the space was and how confined the public was. There was a very large volume of traffic, so that as far as I am concerned I can speak with a certain amount of personal experience. In more recent times I have visited Toronto. I find that the situation has certainly not improved.
I am sure hon. members do not realize the tremendous growth that has taken place in the volume of passenger traffic. Not very long ago I looked at the statistics and I found that in 1936 fewer than 100,000 passengers were carried by the air lines in Canada. The figure for last year was 2,400,000. If the figures are broken down and you look at them by airports, you will find that the major airports, of course, have been the places where the growth in traffic has been most marked. Therefore it is not surprising that the facilities at Dorval and Malton, where the expansion has been particularly pronounced, should no longer be adequate and should require to be replaced.
tMr. Marler.]
I said in my remarks the other day that we were planning to start very shortly on the new terminal at Dorval. So far as Malton is concerned, we have been carrying on discussions with the municipal authorities in Toronto in order to clear up the question on the ownership and title to the land comprising the area. 1 am very pleased to be able to say that I am informed that the municipal council in Toronto has approved the proposals that we have made for the city and that the very important obstacle in the way of the further development at Malton airport has been removed. We hope to be able to undertake the consideration of plans for a new building at Malton just as soon as we can get around to it.
The hon. member spoke about the amount of these two contracts. He thinks the amount is too high. All I may say is that tenders were called on two occasions. The first time tenders were called, the prices were higher than these two, and we called for further bids. It was when tenders were called a second time that the amounts of $72,000, at Dorval, and $40,000 were arrived at as being the lowest tenders for the work. It may be expensive, but I think it is difficult to take the position that the airports are not clean, and so on, and then say we are spending too much to get the work done.

Mr. Chairman, I had not intended to enter this discussion, but I must make some comment about the remarks just made by the minister. There was a complacency about them which was wholly out of keeping with what every one of us has seen in the development of our airport accommodation in this country. When the minister says that we hardly realize the tremendous growth of air traffic, it may be that' there are those who do not. However, the members of this house have had reason to keep themselves informed on this subject and many of them, by the very nature of their activities, are bound to see the evidence of the growth and to participate in the difficulties encountered as a result of the failure to offer accommodation at the exchange points where people change from one aircraft to another. I am not suggesting there are not difficulties, but I would prefer that there were some acceptance of the fact that we are far behind other countries of comparable position in air transport-
Such as?

-in the provision of accommodation at airports. When the minister asks "such as", as though there were any question about it, I think that probably he has seen the Tempelhof airport in Berlin. There is

no airport in this country that even compares with it on a smaller scale. He has probably seen the airport now in operation at Orly in France and the new airport buildings in London, which are not yet completed but which will be incomparably beyond anything in this country. In Milan there is a magnificent airport, beyond anything we have here. In Lisbon, in Portugal, a country much smaller and with relatively little air transport, there is a magnificent airport building. At Schiphol in Holland, a tiny country that would fit within the boundaries of one of our great lakes, there is one of the most magnificent airports in the world. At Geneva, Switzerland-a name that we have been hearing of late very frequently-there is an airport that for accommodation and for finish of structure and general appearance is infinitely beyond anything we now have or now contemplate in this country. In Zurich, in Switzerland, there is an airport that, for cities of the same size in Canada, might well be taken as a model.
Many of the hon. members opposite have been at those airports. The minister of external affairs was in some of them not very long ago. The Minister of Transport says that he has been there too. If he has, he has seen facilities such as we have never attempted to give. One of the ways in which other countries are able to afford these facilities is by leasing space on the premises. If one goes into an airport such as Schiphol or Madrid or Lisbon in countries that we do not think of as comparable to ours in air transportation, one finds good shops and facilities of all kinds. Above all there are good restaurants, excellent restaurants, where one can get meals comparable with any that could be obtained in the best hotels. We have not yet attempted to give facilities of that kind on a basis comparable with any of the airports in any of the capital cities in Europe. In this respect I would say that the capital cities of Europe, are far beyond the capital cities of the United States, heavy though transportation may be there.
One of the things that give this subject importance is that with the long flights in this country and the time that must be spent in airports because of the uncertainty created by weather and other special elements of air transportation, we should have a measure of facilities not yet attempted in Canada. I regret that, in dealing with a situation which has presented its difficulties and which has involved delay, the minister should adopt a complacent tone and seek to leave the impression with the Canadian public that our facilities are in any way comparable with those of the cities of Europe at this time.

Mr. Chairman, there is no complacency whatever on the part of the Department of Transport with regard to the provision of facilities for aviation in Canada. The hon. Leader of the Opposition has pointed to what? He has pointed to the principal airports of the principal countries of Europe. He has talked of Orly, and he has talked of Zurich and a number of other European airports. But in the countries he mentioned, how many major airports are there besides those he has just mentioned?
In Switzerland there are several, and every one of them is better in its accommodation than we have here. I mentioned Geneva and Zurich-

Mr. Chairman, the hon. Leader of the Opposition knows perfectly well that the number of major airports in the European countries is very small. In Denmark there is one major airport, which we had the occasion of seeing. We have seen Orly, and there is another airport at Le Bourget in Paris, but when you look at the situation of the European countries you find that there are very few major airports in each. On the other hand, what is the situation in Canada? We have 20 to 30 major airports. I take it from what the Leader of the Opposition said that we should have terminals comparable to Orly at 20 to 30 places in Canada.
It is indeed amusing to hear the suggestions from the opposition along those lines. When it comes to discussing the amount of expenditures, they are always too high. When it comes to something of this sort they ask, "Why don't you spend more money?" I suggest that the Leader of the Opposition take a realistic view of the expenditures for civil aviation. What has happened in the past? The situation has been that nothing could effectively be done with regard to terminal buildings while the war was on. What has happened since the war? The expenditures for civil aviation have been devoted to runways, to radio aids, to air traffic control facilities, in a word to the essential parts of a system of civil aviation, so that aircraft could operate.
Is it more important to have beautiful buildings or is it more important to have safe conditions for air travel? I suggest that an intelligent policy has been followed by the government with respect to its expenditures for civil aviation. There has been a concentration on the essential facilities while at, the same time the secondary facilities have not been neglected. We all know there are a good many airports in this country which are very good and very satisfactory.

Supply-Transport
I have an idea that, regardless of what the Leader of the Opposition says, the people of Canada will not be disappointed with the idea of having a new airport at Dorval which is to begin this year. We have the plans for a new terminal at Ottawa.
We propose to start the construction of terminal buildings at Quebec and Windsor. The building at Saskatoon has been finished. We are planning for a new building at Winnipeg and at Regina. There is also Gander upon which an early start is to be made. I think that is a rather fair proportion of the budget for civil aviation for this year. I think it is reasonable to suppose that when we have got on further with the provision of radio aids, we shall be able to concentrate more attention on terminal buildings. But I am firmly convinced that those who are interested in air travel prefer to have aircraft to travel in rather than commodious terminal buildings, if a choice must be made between facilities of landing fields on the one hand and commodious buildings on the other.

Mr. Chairman, this specious argument illustrates the way in which the minister has been seeking on a number of items to avoid what has been said. At no point in my remarks did I make any such silly suggestion as he implies, namely that w'e should have 22 Orly airports or London airports here in this country, but I have pointed out that when it comes to the major airports here, they are not comparable with the airports in Europe-
Who compared them?

-and that the impression that we have actually kept pace is in itself out of keeping with reality.
The fact is that we have heavy air transportation here. This country at one time carried the largest-not in percentage though-air freight transportation in the world. We have been pioneers in the air field. All I am saying is that instead of this complacent attitude of the minister in which he disposes of any suggestion of this kind in the way that he does, he should recognize that we have not kept pace. His remark to the effect that those flying would rather have aircraft than commodious accommodation is, of course, just a childish comment with regard to quite an important subject. There is not a single person who is flying who does not want good aircraft.
And good airfields.

But every person who is flying wants to have reasonable accommodation, if he can get it. Anybody who is flying in Canada knows perfectly well that there is

great need for improvement in the airports. What I was suggesting-and all I was suggesting-was that with the evidence before us as to the type of facilities offered in the capital cities of Europe, we might well use some imagination in building new airports here. When he says that the people of Canada will not object to a new airport at Dorval, may I say that they certainly will not. That has been a very poor entrance to Canada for a long time. The people of Canada will welcome a good airport there. But when the minister talks about the opposition asking for economies and then suggesting expenditures, may I tell him that we have day by day seen evidence of money wasted by this extravagant government.
Oh, oh.

That money might well be put into proper things. Before the minister makes comments of this kind, let him in his mind just go back to the William Carson and the way in which they tossed millions of dollars around there without much regard. If some of the money that was wasted in that case were spent in providing appropriate facilities at proper points for airports here, Canadians might feel that they had something to show for the money that has been spent across this country. I am not asking for any extravagance. All I am asking for is that this government, instead of simply adopting the complacent attitude that the minister shows, should look to what has been accomplished elsewhere and then, in building new airports here, should provide some of those excellent facilities which are available in the countries of Europe at this time.
We hear talk about the fact that we in this country must, of course, remember that there are only a few airports. Of course there are. But as the minister knows, in Switzerland there is limited air transportation compared with ours because it is a small country very largely occupied by high mountains. But the two main airports at Geneva and Zurich are incomparably better in their accommodation than any airport in Canada although we are one of the major countries in the world in air transportation. We are not asking this government to keep up with the Joneses. We are not asking them to be extravagant in this respect. We are asking them to spend their money well and, when they build new airports, to provide some of these modern and up-to-date facilities which, along with good aircraft, well manned, do bring the people to the airports and help make the stay at the airports as attractive and as comfortable as possible. The minister himself has indicated that he knows what

these delays may mean. Let us make sure that with the money spent we provide facilities in keeping with the nature of this great transportation for which Canada is so peculiarly suited. I would hope that when suggestions are made to the minister, he would not deny the reputation he has had on other occasions for his competence in other fields by the supercilious attitude he has shown on this occasion.
Oh, oh.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to come back to the item which precipitated this discussion which has gone so far afield, namely provision of $112,000 for a cleaning contract founded on the government's making attempts, however feeble the Leader of the Opposition may think they are, to save money here and there. The question I should like to ask the minister is this. What assurance have we that, in letting this particular work out to contract, and therefore, as the minister states, saving money, it is not being done at the expense of having people working at lower wages and under poorer working conditions than would have prevailed had the work been done by civil servants?

Mr. Chairman, I think that the labour laws of the country certainly afford the necessary protection to those who are engaged by the contractors. I take it that in the one case it is the laws of Ontario and in the other case it would be the laws of Quebec. I have never heard it said in Quebec that the laws did not give adequate protection in the matter of minimum wages and specified labour rates in urban places like Montreal and Toronto.
On page 95 I notice that last year 18 charwomen were employed. I see that they are not employed this year. Is that situation the result of this subletting out?
Yes.
Are those women to be replaced or is there any such assurance?
I take it that they will be replaced by employees of the contractors.

499. Construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and new equipment, including construction work on municipal airports, $14,240,050.

I should like to draw the minister's attention to the fact that at the Yorkton airport the peacetime continuation of an air force training school which was established during the war has served a very useful purpose in that community. The people are most appreciative of the service 50433-416
Supply-Transport
that has been given. The T.C.A. services there have been valuable to the people in that community. The one trouble is that the runways there are rather short for the landing of aircraft of any considerable size. I have been given to understand that this year it is intended to enlarge one of these runways and that this improvement will require the acquisition of additional property. I was wondering whether it was the intention of the department to proceed with that construction this year. Can he tell us whether surveys have been made, whether the new land has been acquired, whether or not any tenders have been let, and what amount is expected to be spent on this improvement?

I might tell the hon. member that in the case of the airport at Yorkton we have three items of work which it is proposed to carry out in the coming year. First of all, there is the installation of low intensity approach lights as an aid for night flying, at an approximate cost of $30,000. Then there is taxiway lighting on the east taxiway as a further aid for night flying, at a cost of approximately $6,000. Then it is proposed to extend runway 0321 to 4,800 feet and to widen it to 150 feet. At present the runway is not serviceable in the spring break-up, and it is required to lengthen it to the figure I have mentioned in order to provide for standard operations. I am not perfectly certain whether or not the land has been acquired. I may say though that it is the intention of the department to try to proceed with the work either in the latter part of August or perhaps September.

Has the contract been
advertised?
I think the answer to that is no.
Will the extension of the runway require the closing off of a municipal roadway?

I am afraid it is a little difficult, without having the plans of the runway before me, to know whether or not that will be necessary, but if the hon. member is interested I shall be glad to make inquiries and let him know.
What is the estimate for the total expenditure on the complete project?
I hope that the outside figure will be no more than $350,000. That is, of course, for the runway.

The Yorkton airport is
situated about halfway between Winnipeg and Saskatoon directly on the course of flights between those places. I think it is very valuable to have it there in case of

emergency and that the facilities the minister has outlined will make the airport very much appreciated.

On this item I should like to say to the Minister of Transport how grateful the people of Halifax are for the fine consideration he and the department have given to the need of an airport at Halifax and, for that matter, all other transportation facilities serving Halifax. Has the minister any recent information regarding the progress being made on the Halifax airport? Can he say whether the city of Halifax has cleared the titles for all the land, whether sufficient land has been acquired and when the work will actually start?

There is provision in the main estimates for an amount of $50,000 and in the supplementaries for an amount of $450,000 for the new airport at Halifax. We hope it will be possible to commence the work on this site in the fall, particularly the clearing, so that we may be able to get on with the work as soon as possible.

What is the position with regard to the Vancouver airport? Before the session opened the lower mainland members were asked by the airport committee to meet with them and discuss the situation with respect to the Vancouver airport. As the minister perhaps knows, over a period of years there has been a question whether the Vancouver airport should remain under the actual ownership of the city of Vancouver or should be acquired by the federal government. I understand that the matter is still very much under discussion. I should like to ask the minister whether negotiations for the transfer of ownership from the city of Vancouver to the federal government are still in mind, whether the Minister of Transport is interested and, if so, just how far he is prepared to go in making a proper payment for the purchase of the airport. I should like to know whether the airport is to remain in the ownership of the city of Vancouver or is going to be transferred to the federal government.
What are the plans with respect to development of the airport? We were told at the time of the meeting I mentioned a few moments ago that on account of the growth of the city of Vancouver and international air travel and the amount of commercial traffic, light plane flying and R.C.A.F. flying a great many millions of dollars would have to be spent on the airport within the next ten years. I should like to know not only what is going to be done within the next twelve months but whether the Department of Transport is

pursuing a long range over-all plan or whether it is simply proceeding on a year to year basis and only doing what it figures it can get away with or is immediately necessary. Because of the importance of Vancouver airport to all of Canada, I believe we should have a definite understanding of what is in the mind of the minister.

I am happy to tell the hon. member that there is a long-term plan for the further development of the airport at Vancouver and that I think no one would contest for an instant the importance of the airport at Vancouver either in domestic aviation or in international aviation. The hon. member referred first of all to the question of offers that had been made to the city by my department in the past. My understanding is that those offers were submitted, but I believe that it was required that municipal action of some kind be taken. I believe there was a referendum in which the necessary majority was not obtained in order that the transaction could be consummated. Since then we have not pressed the city of Vancouver to do anything further.
I do not mind saying that I do not think it is material whether the Vancouver airport is owned by the city or by my department. At the present time the city is operating it with very great efficiency and, quite candidly, I do not believe we would operate it more efficiently than the city. Moreover, I understand that the city is also making money out of the operation, which no doubt is helpful to the city finances.
For this year we are proposing to spend $560,000 on the airport. The principal expenditures are for aircraft parking and loading aprons for which the current year's expenditure is expected to be $200,000 out of an estimated total of about $390,000. In addition, it is proposed to build a taxiway to runway 0826. The cost of the taxiway is estimated to be slightly less than $600,000 and the anticipated expenditure during the current year will be about $300,000. Then there are certain other minor expenditures. I might mention particularly a taxiway to the hangar area to cost $40,000, with the current expenditure to be $20,000. There are one or two other details that make up the total of $560,000. I hope I have answered all the questions the hon. member has asked. If I have not, I shall be glad to do so.

There is one other phase I might mention which I did refer to indirectly.
I refer to the problem of light aircraft using Vancouver airport. Is there any plan under way now for the acquisition or development of a secondary airport in the Vancouver area to

be used by all light aircraft? This is now a very serious problem in the lower mainland region.

Ever since I have been minister of the department, it has been constantly drawn to my attention how desirable it would be to have a secondary field at Vancouver. The difficulty appears to have been to find a site that is satisfactory in all respects. I can only tell my hon. friend that there are a couple of sites now under active consideration and I hope that we may have something to report later on in the year. I cannot say anything more definite than that just at this time.

In this connection, as the minister has said, there has been considerable concern about getting a secondary airport for Vancouver. Certain recommendations have been made by groups who are interested in flying. The minister has just mentioned that there are two sites under consideration.
I take it that one of those sites is what is known as Spanish banks; is that correct?

Yes, I understand that that site has been suggested to the department. The department has passed on this information to the Vancouver airport board, the municipal body, and we have asked them to express their observations on this site. I think that is where the matter stands at the moment. If the hon. member has any suggestions to make, knowing his familiarity with that part of the country, I would certainly welcome those suggestions.

I should like to point out to the minister that the residents of that district are greatly upset about this suggestion. I realize, as well as anybody else, the need for a secondary airport. Spanish banks is the finest beach in greater Vancouver. Probably today there would be several thousand people from Vancouver, tourists from the western states and people visiting from the interior of British Columbia right out on that beach. It is just below the university area where a great many new homes are to be built. There is property there which has been subdivided already and is awaiting action by the provincial government to sell it, so there will be thousands more people living right within a stone's throw of this proposed site. The residents are greatly upset.
I have here a copy of the Vancouver Province for Tuesday, July 19, which contains an article with the heading: "Danger to Famous Beach-Residents at Spanish banks to protest airport proposal". It was in these waters that the ships of Captain Vancouver and the Spanish Captain Quadra met nearly 200 years ago. As a matter of fact, it is 50433-416J

from this Captain Quadra that the riding I have the honour to represent gets its name. It would be a great mistake, I believe, to put an auxiliary airport right on this beach. The minister may very well get favourable recommendations from the people he is consulting in Vancouver because they are people who are interested in flying. I would ask him to keep in mind that such a development might do untold harm to the residents in that portion of the city of Vancouver, not only at the present time but in the future. In reply to these remarks I should like to say that some representations, much in the same sense, have been made to my department. Without knowing the geography, I must say I have felt rather sympathetic to them personally. I understand that there are two aldermen on the municipal airport board, and I take it they would be very sensitive to the opinions of the people who would be affected.

I should like to ask the minister about the Lethbridge airport. The people of Lethbridge are not anxious to have anything more than is coming to them but they are anxious to have all that is coming to them. I should like the minister to make a statement to the committee as to whether or not the Lethbridge airport is up to full standard, bearing in mind the population of the city, its geographical location and its importance in the air travel of Canada.

Supply-Transport
out to them the hope that something will be done during the current year that will be of interest to them.

What we are particularly concerned about, Mr. Chairman, is whether or not the runways are long enough and adequate to permit of servicing the finest flying planes that wish to settle at Lethbridge temporarily.

I understand from my officials that the runways are approximately 5,000 feet long, and as the hon. member knows that is sufficient to accommodate DC-3's and aircraft of that character but not of course the larger planes which require about 6,000 feet. My understanding of the matter is that, for the moment at least, it is not contemplated that we should extend the runways, but that depends very much on the traffic. Where there is a demand for longer runways because the traffic is there to justify them, we look at the applications with a great deal of sympathy.

My question pertains to Malton. In February, 1954, the Department of Transport expropriated about 14 lots at Malton together with the houses that were either completely or partly constructed. Then, weeks later the properties were turned back to the original owners. Apparently the department did not require some of them at least, and that resulted in a number of claims for compensation. Can the minister tell me whether those claims have all been settled? If so, what was the total amount of those claims?

I am afraid I cannot give the hon. member the total amount of the claims. My understanding is that substantially all of them have been settled. If the hon. member would like to have more precise information I think I can procure it for him, but I do not have it in my possession at the moment.

Could the minister let
me have the amount? I do not want the individual amounts but I would like to know the total amount of the claims that have been settled. The minister said, I believe, that substantially all of them have.
Yes.

I would like to know
which ones have not been settled, to date. Then would the minister indicate the justification for expropriating these lots and then, six weeks later, giving them back.

I understand that when the
expropriation was first filed representations were made to the department by a number
[Mr. Marler.l
of home owners that this action was going to affect materially the living accommodation of other home owners in the immediate vicinity. We revised our plans for the development of Malton in order to try to accommodate them. But then, when the matter was re-examined, it was found that the best thing to do was to expropriate all of them. And that is actually what has been done.

Do I understand that
these were eventually expropriated?
Yes, so I understand.
Since when? These were turned back to the original owners within six weeks after the expropriation order.

I am informed that what I
said is correct. Those who had first objected then said they would like to have the department take over their property, after all; and settlements with them were negotiated.

With respect to the matter
raised by the hon. member for York South, although not dealing with the lots he mentioned which, I understand, belong to one subdivider, I would direct my remarks to the same expropriation order which was filed in the registry office of the county of Peel on February 12, 1954, and which affected 164 separate parcels of land.
In answer to a question of mine on May 4 I was advised that, of the 164 parcels of land affected, only 32 transactions had been completed. That is over the year, from the time that the owners of these lands were deprived of their ownership. No compensation had been paid to them some 15 months later. As recently as June 30 I wrote to the minister requesting additional information as to how many of these transactions had been completed. Although I had a letter in reply saying that the information would be obtained, up to this time I have not received that information.
I suggest this is a serious problem, because many of these are individual home owners who have been deprived of the ownership of their homes, without compensation, and they are therefore deprived of the opportunity to relocate. They are deprived of the benefit of the increase in value of their homes, if the economy of the country is expanding, as we are told by hon. members who support the government.
Do you not think so?

Replying to that I would say that I did not make a speech on the budget, but perhaps I could agree that there is an expanding economy.

They are deprived of the natural gain that would be theirs, although they have the use of the homes in the meantime. But I think it indicates complete disregard by the department of the little person. These are not big home owners; only small homes are involved. There are some large tracts of land involved, lands owned by farmers over the years, and perhaps they are continuing their normal operations. But there are also a large number of very small home owners affected.
I suggest that the treatment given to them by the department, through its laxity in making settlement, is just a little brutal. I do not think any member in the house would like to be put in the same position, that of having something taken forcibly from him, and no compensation paid.
The figures speak for themselves. As of May 4, of the 164 parcels of land, only 32 transactions had been completed, and 10 others expected to be completed shortly. In respect of that 164 parcels, only 125 valuations had been made at that time. The result is that 39 persons are still sitting there, without the department's even having evaluated their lands. It may be that that is the attitude the government thinks it should take. It may be that the government feels that they do not need to worry about the little fellow. But I suggest to the minister that this is a matter of some importance. If the people who are handling it are not capable of completing the transactions, and if there is too much work around other airports for them to do, then they should get someone who could handle it, someone who could complete it, or get more people in to do the job.
After all, in common with most people, I would imagine that most of these home owners are carrying mortgages; their mortgages are maturing. Where are they going to get the money to pay them off? Then, some of them are holders under the Veterans' Land Act. What is the situation there? The authorities under the Veterans' Land Act say they want all their money. So far as I know, no serious intervention has been made by the Department of Transport in an effort to mitigate the damages or to mitigate the loss that would be occasioned those veterans.
It may be that this is a subject which affects people who, in the great swirl of millions handled by the department, are not considered important. But I do draw to the minister's attention the fact that 18 months have elapsed since the expropriation was filed, and that as of now some hundreds of claims have not been paid. Let me add this,
Supply-Transport
that I have had meetings with these people and have found all of them quite reasonable. A person who was doing the job properly could settle every claim in a week, and do>
it satisfactorily. I know the amounts of the claims made by these people, and they are not unreasonable.
If the person or persons in the department were doing their job properly every one of these claims could now be settled and paid, and it could all be done, at the very outside, in two weeks from this date. Not one person in the group is unreasonable, and I have talked to practically all of them.

So far as I am concerned, and so far as my department is concerned, we fully understand that when it is necessary to expropriate land in the vicinity of airports it does represent a very real inconvenience to those who are expropriated. We fully realize that in many instances it is a very disrupting factor for the proprietors who are concerned.
In the present instance, respecting the 164 parcels of land, I may say that the settlements are being effected. I would like to see them effected more rapidly. I believe I signed four or five applications to treasury board this week in respect of current expropriations; and almost every week additional ones are coming in. I should just like to say this, too, Mr. Chairman. The policy which we endeavour to follow in these expropriations is to pay the owner a fair price for his property. My departmental officials know that we do not wish at any time to take advantage of the time factor, the superior resources of the government, or any other factor, to take undue advantage of any owner. Perhaps I should not say "any undue advantage". I do not mean to take advantage at all of the owners who are affected.
I would point out to the hon. member that there are frequently differences of opinioni as to whether a settlement is reasonable or not, but I, rightly or wrongly, have been inclined to take the attitude that we should try to give the owner expropriated the benefit of the doubt. I would point out that there are; some cases where we are unable to reach an agreement with the owner and in those cases the owner of course must apply to the courts for redress. As I understand it, when the award is given the judgment allows interest on the indemnity from the time of the expropriation. I should like to go further and say that in a number of cases that have come before me where the owner wished to obtain in advance of a final settlement some payment on account, we have been glad to make payment.

If the hon. member knows of cases where the payment, in his judgment, ought to be made, I would be very glad if he would bring them to the attention of the department and we shall try to give them the most sympathetic consideration. I fully understand that when expropriations take place we should endeavour, so far as reasonably possible, to mitigate the effects so far as the owner is concerned.
With respect to the last statement about drawing to the attention of the department matters-

No, I am sorry; the hon. member misunderstood what I said. What I wanted to say to him was that if he knew of cases where an advance payment would mitigate the difficulties, if he would draw those particular cases to the attention of the department I would try to accommodate them.
Mr. Pallet!: With respect to the last statement about advance payments, I would remind the minister that I have drawn to his attention certain instances where advance payments would mitigate difficulties, and as recently as last Saturday, a week ago tomorrow, such payments had not been made.
Would the hon. member mind giving me privately the name and I shall look into it?
Yes.

Mr. Chairman, while we are on this subject may I say I went into that case particularly on behalf of some of those properties which had been returned after the expropriation. It seemed to me there was very poor business management somewhere. The department expropriated a large slice of land and registered the expropriation order on February 19. A few weeks later the owners were notified by mail that the expropriation order was to be abandoned. That was on March 30, I think, and abandonment of the expropriation order was registered in the registry office. Over a year after that, some of the people who had houses half constructed on their lots were still waiting for settlement. Their creditors were pressing. I was in touch with the departmental officials off and on throughout that year, and last spring, while we were in session here -it must have been March or April-I was informed by one of the officials that everything was ready to settle those claims but no money had yet been voted by parliament toward settlement.
When was this?
That was a year after the expropriation order had been issued.
Does that mean 1955 or 1954?

The expropriation was in 1954. In 1955, while this house was in session and before the budget was passed, I was told that no money had been voted by parliament to make those settlements. It does not look to me like good business to expropriate land, and then a year later discover that no money had been provided for the payment and to keep people waiting. The minister can tell me whether those claims are all settled yet or not, or whether some of them are still outstanding.

It is my understanding that the settlement negotiated was concluded in March, before the end of the last fiscal year, and at that time we did not have funds in the budget that could serve in connection with the settlement. My understanding is that when this year's budget is passed it will be found possible to complete the payment of the settlement, or at least complete the arrangements that were made.
I think the hon. member referred to the case of a number of individual owners. My understanding of it is that they were not the actual registered owners of the properties in some instances, but had made arrangements with the subdivider, and it is with the subdivider owner of the property that our settlement is being concluded. I take it that just as soon as we have carried out our part of the bargain with the subdivider he will be able to carry out his arrangements with the persons who are affected and who form part of the property that he had subdivided.
Mr. Pallet!: I have one further question on this item. Is any allowance made under this item for claims for damages under regulation P.C. 1953-546? This is the regulation that controls the use of the lands adjacent to the airport, and contains this very interesting clause:
No person shall operate or cause to be operated on any lands to which these regulations apply any machine, device, contrivance or thing after being notified by the minister that, in the opinion of the minister, the machine, device, contrivance or thing causes or is likely to cause, by the emission of light, smoke, noise or fumes, a hazard of obstruction to aircraft using the airport.
It seems to me that a regulation of this kind would certainly very seriously depreciate the lands on which it is registered. Has provision been made in these estimates for the payment of claims for damages occasioned?

I do not think the hon. member is right in saying that these things depreciate the property, but they do in some instances

occasion damage to the people who are affected by the zoning regulations. My understanding is that under the Aeronautics Act there is a provision by which such people are entitled to claim compensation for the damages. That is, of course, one of the necessary consequences of the zoning regulations.

I appreciate that, Mr. Chairman. But in view of the fact that, as I understand it, a number of claims for damages have been filed, I am wondering whether any provision is made in the estimates to pay the damages if they are allowed? We have had one instance this morning of the fact that there was no money to pay for lands expropriated. Is the same situation going to arise here?

My understanding, Mr. Chairman, is that the provision of funds is made when the damages have been determined before the exchequer court. I understand that has always been the practice.
Mr. Pallet!: It would not appear in the estimates, then, until next year?
I understand that, if there is a judgment of the exchequer court, we can obtain an advance of funds for the purpose of meeting it.

The item to which I want to refer is an extension to the runway at the airport at Charlottetown. The extension is supposed to bring the runway up to DC-3 standards, which would make it acceptable. I should point out that the project for which we have been asking in Charlottetown for some time is for a longer runway that will provide landing facilities for larger aircraft. The proposed extension to the runway will not do that. Because it will abut against a much travelled roadway it will be incapable of being extended further. I was not so happy about the proposed extension to the runway when I first learned of it, as I felt it might prejudice our chances of getting the longer runway later. But, after having discussed it with the minister and his deputy, I do not think that is the case.
I do not think I could discuss this Charlottetown airport development without mentioning the story of a young man who developed a company, the development of which is so closely tied in with the airport that they are almost synonymous. I am talking about Captain Carl Burke who in 1942 organized the Maritime Central Airways, commonly known as M.C.A. From a very small and humble beginning, this young man and his company have achieved outstanding success. Last year the company carried 65,000 passengers, flew some 3 million miles and carried 4,200 tons of
Supply-Transport
freight. Those are round figures. I learned today that this year they expect to double, or perhaps triple, their freight-carrying performance of 1954.
Today M.C.A. is the largest independent air freight operator in Canada. Indeed it ranks only behind T.C.A. in the matter of air freight transport. I understand it now has an application before the air transport board for a transatlantic freight charter. Very recently M.C.A. acquired in Moncton a large hangar that had previously been owned by T.C.A. In the immediate future it will have its maintenance depot there. I understand the company is planning to set up a large maintenance organization at Moncton to handle the servicing there of its new heavy aircraft of the DC-4 and C-46 type.
The company has one of the finest safety records that can be found anywhere. I do not think it can be surpassed. I think I am correct in saying that it has not had a single fatality on its passenger service. I cannot even recall a serious accident to a passenger plane. In 1953 air line passenger traffic in and out of Charlottetown alone amounted to over 23,000 passengers. Air passenger and air transport traffic at Charlottetown have increased by more than 400 per cent during the last 10 years, and there are indications that the upward trend will continue.
With such a splendid record of development, expansion and achievement, with such an unparalleled safety record, it seems too bad that this young man who started the development and who has been largely responsible for its growth should have to move the maintenance hangar to another city. This company, organized and developed by this Charlottetown man, has moved the major part of its maintenance from Charlottetown to Moncton.
I could give you many other reasons why we are in need of runways in Charlottetown that will accommodate larger planes. However, I discussed this question fully with the minister and his senior officials. Our board of trade was very helpful in pressing our claim. I must say that I have had very satisfactory talks with the minister about this. My idea is that this is not the time to press for this longer runway, but I should like to think that the minister is keeping our need in mind. I hope that in the not too far distant future we can look forward to some concrete action in this matter. I think, if I have interpreted the minister's feelings correctly, perhaps we are not far apart, but I should like to hear his reaction.

Mr. Chairman, before I had had an opportunity to discuss the matter very fully with the hon. member, my officials had

recommended to me that we should include a provision in the estimates for the extension of the runway, which I understand is now about 2,800 feet, to a length of 4,000 feet. I have since had the opportunity of talking to the hon. member, and it seemed to me that there were some real advantages in providing a runway which would accommodate aircraft of the DC-3 standard. I therefore urged him to withhold for the moment the request for the longer runway which would accommodate larger aircraft. I think this is a sensible development, and I think it could assure him that the extension of the runway this year will not prejudice his case for a longer runway for heavier aircraft when the need develops.

Mr. Chairman, I believe this item of approximately $14|- million represents the largest amount that we have had to consider so far and is an increase of $3,314,775 over the amount asked for last year. Before the item carries I should like to go back to a couple of questions dealing with Malton. In the July 21 issue of the Globe and Mail I notice a statement attributed to the minister. It may have been part of what he said to the house. The statement to which I refer is as follows:
Mr. Marler said his department has had discussions with civic authorities concerning Malton and Toronto island airport and-
This is in quotation marks.
-"we believe that at an early date the obstacles to the further development of Malton will be removed."
I wonder whether the minister will let us know what the obstacles are in this case? I specifically ask him this question because in the press there has been some reference to the fact that some members of the city council of the city of Toronto feel that they are handing over to the federal government title to the Malton airport with a very hazy promise of some sort that they are going to have certain things done for them in the future. I would therefore ask these questions: What are these obstacles? How soon does the minister expect they will be removed? Thereafter, how soon does he expect construction to start on the additional facilities at Malton airport?

Mr. Chairman, when I spoke the other day about obstacles I had in mind particularly the fact that although we have been carrying on discussions with the municipal authorities for some little time we had had at that time-that was the day before yesterday-no information to the effect that the city council of Toronto had approved the proposals which we had submitted. I read in the paper, I think the night before last, that the city council had approved the proposals which we had submitted, so that I think I might say that that obstacle of council approval has now disappeared.
I should like to say to my hon. friend that the proposals which we have made to the city council are not vague. They are clear-cut and definite. They were embodied in a letter addressed by me I think to Mayor Phillips, and I think that they were perfectly clear. I think that agreement between Toronto and

the department has now been reached. I am not certain just offhand exactly what steps must be taken to implement the understanding. I think my hon. friend will understand the sort of thing that will have to be done when I tell him that, as I understand the situation at the present time, approximately one-third of the Malton airport has the title vested in the city of Toronto and not in the department itself and that there is no written arrangement of any kind between the city and the department. My hon. friend being a lawyer, I am quite sure he will realize that is not the kind of situation which members of the legal profession are inclined to commend to their clients. I realize that perhaps the relations between the department and the city of Toronto are not quite on the same plane as the relations between private individuals. The city having now come to this decision, I hope that the detailed procedural arrangements can be carried out without delay. I think that the Toronto newspapers have faithfully reported the substance of the proposals which were made to the city; and I must say that-having looked at them myselr-I think the proposals have been very fair to the city. I hope it will be possible to give effect to them without further delay and to clear up a situation which I think must be considered to have been unsatisfactory in so far as the title was concerned.

Mr. Chairman, I specifically referred to this question because I rather tied in the obstacles which were mentioned here to the further item in the report that it might be or would be necessary to make temporary improvements at Malton pending this permanent construction.

I perhaps might explain,
Mr. Chairman, that there is no connection between these two things at all. Not knowing that the city council in Toronto had approved the proposals which we had made- in point of fact I think they were approved the same day that I made the remarks in the house-what I said was that we hoped to conclude these arrangements as soon as the obstacles were removed although it would be some time before we could have a new terminal building at Malton, but in the meanwhile that we were proposing to make some temporary improvements to alleviate the congestion which exists there now. There is no connection between the two things.

Is there any specific target date for the start on construction of the new terminal facilities at Malton? What apparently caused the discussion in the city council was the fact that there was no
Supply-Transport
feeling of unanimity that they had a specific promise of a time of commencement of this work.

I am sorry but I have not in my possession at the moment a copy of my letter to the mayor. However, I may say to my hon. friend that there is no commitment as to the date. But it is our hope to make a start this year on the planning of the terminal building. I do not think it would be wise for me to say at this moment and at this stage of the situation just when we shall be able to commence operations. However, I may assure members of the committee that we are conscious of the need for better facilities at Malton. I hope that we shall be able to provide them even before it might be expected of us to be able to do so.

I have just a few closing remarks to make in this connection. When the general discussion was taking place concerning the requirements for new airport facilities, I notice that reference was made to the fact that a great many of the airports were completed in the early war years of the war or before the war and that naturally the government could not be expected to have thought of this post-war development.
I might point out to the minister that Malton had a substantial building put up since the war. There is a familiar expression to the effect that it is easy to have hindsight. However, the situation appears to indicate a certain lack of vision or we might have prepared for the conditions which exist today. In other words, having had the new building put up within the last seven years or eight years,-and I do not even know whether it is that long ago- we are now faced with a situation in which we are going to require, I would say, immense additional facilities. I would submit to the minister that he might at this time take into account the fact that in Toronto there is considerable hope that Malton airport will be developed into one of the greatest international airports in the world. I would think that he should be aiming to provide the facilities which were referred to as existing at important international airports in other countries. If this type of vision is not used, I say to the minister that we shall be back here again within the next four or five years asking for additional money for a new or an additional type of building.
This is only one phase of vision which may have to be used in this connection. Of course I might say that, if the present system of monopoly continues, we might never have

Supply-Transport
an international airport in Toronto. But I do not think we can assume that it will always be the attitude of the present government or of any other government to pursue that course. But in connection with complete development of airports everywhere in this country, I am hopeful that the minister and his department are as up to date as possible with regard to the latest principles of aerodynamic design. We read today of the new theories of boundary layer control which indicate that perhaps in the foreseeable future vast extensions of airport runways to 6,000, 7,000 or 8,000 feet may, for all useful purposes, not be necessary. There must be an indication somewhere in the department where the line can be drawn. I would think that the planning must surely be at least 10 years in advance. If that type of policy is pursued, then I think there can be a great saving to the people of the country in this type of construction.

All I should like to say to my hon. friend is that I fully realize the necessity of planning well into the future. We are trying to think in terms of 15 years, but if my hon. friend has a crystal ball that goes farther than that we could use it.

I am wondering if the department is satisfied that this type of program is producing an adequate number of pilots for the air force. I would think that should be a very specific goal of the program. As I understand the situation in the United States, the preliminary part of the training involving the weeding out process, shall we say, is to a great extent handed over to civilian operated schools. crew through this subsidized program. Has there been any liaison between the two which would enable early weeding out before great expense is involved in qualifying people as jet pilots later on in the air force? Have there been any discussions on that matter at all?

I think I can dispose of that very simply. I think the hon. member should realize that this program is designed primarily to produce civilian pilots and not military or naval pilots. 501. Contributions to municipalities or public bodies for construction and improvements of airports on land acquired by such organizations, $136,000.

I should like to say a few words on this item but as it is after one o'clock, Mr. Chairman, I would ask you to call it one o'clock.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

I want to make one of my session-ending Lilliputian speeches on this item. I want to refer to the necessity for more grants for the development of these supplementary or feeder airports. The department has done some excellent work in the development of the airports in this country, and in recent years has expended approximately $200,000 on the Castlegar airport, which is an excellent airport. The excellence and efficiency of this airport is the result of co-operative planning between the municipal committee and the officials of the minister's department. It is a great asset to the district and is much appreciated. The airports at Cranbrook, Castlegar and Penticton form a chain of airports along the southern route of British Columbia and provide excellent service for the people of that area.
Supply-Transport
However, having said that, I want to bring to the minister's attention the necessity for the further development of these supplementary or feeder airports, quite small airports.
I think they are particularly necessary in mountainous country such as that which I represent. Now, the pontoon planes which are usually used in the forest service, the mining industry and the lumbering industry and by people generally, operate very satisfactorily in normal weather, but in rough weather, particularly in the spring and fall months when the lakes are rough, planes of this type find it difficult to operate for days at a time. For that reason, we require the development of these small supplementary airports that provide landing fields for land planes.
These supplementary fields are of great value to the forest industry, the mining industry, the residents of the district and tourists. In recent years there has been a tremendous development, and just to inform the minister of recent events and to illustrate the necessity, on the 20th of this month the government of British Columbia announced there was a forest management licence granted to the Celgar corporation for over
758,000	acres along the Columbia river. The proposal is to build a pulp plant worth $30 million. Within these areas there is an equal production by all the small operators in the district, and an expanding production. There are great developments in the mining industry. I can think of one mine at the present time which uses air service considerably and that is the Sunshine Lardeau in the north Lardeau district. There is an increasing tourist traffic every year. The production of the woods, of the mines and on the land is increasing very rapidly. We live in an expanding economy in the southeastern portion of British Columbia, in every sense of the word.
In order to meet that need satisfactorily I do believe there should be grants made for the development of these smaller airports. They are confined, of course, to locations where they can be suitably provided, and those locations are limited in mountainous country such as ours. But we do need them at Nelson and at Kaslo, and we want the one at Selmo, which is now owned by the department, maintained and kept serviceable. We certainly need one at Revelstoke to service the lumber industry and other industries south of there. I am quite sure the hon. member representing the Revelstoke area will have something to say on that. I would support his request for a grant of $12,500 for the further development of the Revelstoke airport. I know these people individually, and remember when that airport was first started.

Supply-Transport
For a small community, the people of Revel-stoke have done a great deal on their own in the development of that airport, and deserve every encouragement from the department.
In addition to that, it will be very necessary to have that airport developed because of the expanding lumber industry, and the developments in that area and the Big Bend country, and to service those mining and forest industries that lie to the south in my constituency. Revelstoke is on the main line of the Canadian Pacific and frequently mining operators and lumber operators find it necessary to fly to Revelstoke to catch a train or to fly spare parts to Revelstoke or fly spare parts from Revelstoke for machinery in order to maintain their production without loss of time. This morning I listened with interest to the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition. I think his remarks illustrate to some extent the fact that he is not in as close touch with the rank and file as simple people like myself. If I heard him correctly, he advocated the further development of our large airports, which I would support where it was necessary, but I say before we go in for magnificence and the imitating of, what shall I say, the advertising features of European airports in Canada, we could better spend that money on the development of the necessary smaller supplementary airports in this country which are so necessary and which are a vital link in air transportation in a country such as ours. They are becoming increasingly necessary to those who are carrying on in those areas.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, with these few brief remarks I urge the minister to give serious consideration to the development of these smaller fields, in some cases requiring a very small amount of money, in his future estimates in the interests of those who are responsible for economic developments in that type of country.

I greatly regret that any remarks add to the necessity of making further comments at this stage of the proceedings, but I do not intend to let the inaccurate impression remain on the record that has just been put there. There was not one word in what I said this morning that suggested I was advocating the building of palatial airports and seeking to exclude from consideration the smaller airports. I think perhaps there are those who know I have had fairly extensive contact with the smaller airports throughout this country as well as the larger ones. Perhaps there is no one, from his personal background or from his immediate [Mr. Herridge.l
requirements in ordinary transportation, who would be more interested in seeing the smaller airports developed to the very limit. I have always advocated that in this country, with its unique opportunity for air development, we should do everything we can to stress the development of flying, whether it be in the larger centres or in the smaller centres.
I do not wish to extend the remarks I have already made beyond emphasizing that in these larger centres, where there is a great concentration of aircraft and where airports must be built in any event, we should take advantage of the experience that has produced such excellent results elsewhere. We have a record second to none in air transportation; but the one place where, unquestionably, it is open to criticism is in the matter of the facilities provided. It is only necessary for anyone to fly across this country today, and change from one aircraft to another, or to travel on one of the sidelines, to find that the accommodation offered to the passenger who is waiting is certainly not in keeping with the standards of air service itself, or in fact with modern practices in regard to transportation of any kind.
My remarks were in that direction; and nothing I said implied that I was seeking to concentrate in a few palatial airports such moneys as would be spent in the development of air facilities in this country.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make only one or two comments in regard to item 501. First of all I should like to express my appreciation of the grant to the municipal corporation of the town of Meadow Lake for the construction of an airport at that point. I find, too, that in item 770 of the supplementary estimates there is a further sum for this same purpose.
Over the years Meadow Lake has been the centre for the development of northern Saskatchewan. This condition runs back well over a hundred years, to the time when it was known, in the days of fur trading, as Bolsover House. For a short time Meadow Lake relinquished that distinction to a point known as Green Lake, 35 miles to the east but in the same general area. The Hudson's Bay Company used Green Lake as a marshalling yard for all northern Saskatchewan, including part of eastern Alberta and the lake Athabasca area.
Some little while ago I was privileged to talk to an old gentleman who used to do the freighting from Minneapolis to Green Lake. This was done by the use of horses,, over a distance of about 1,400 miles, and

then another 1,400 or 1,500 miles travelling up the various rivers into the lake Athabasca area.
It is clear therefore that this part of Saskatchewan surrounding Meadow Lake has been associated with the far north for over a hundred years. It is fitting therefore that this item should now appear in the estimates, so that Meadow Lake may continue to play a leading part. I have no doubt that, so far as transport is concerned, it will justify the grant as set out in item 501. It is the point farthest north in Saskatchewan on a railway line. As such it is closer by 100 miles than any other point with rail facilities to the uranium and other mineral areas in the lake Athabasca region. As I have said, I have no doubt that in years to come it will justify this expenditure.
Before taking my seat may I commend the minister not only upon his action in this connection but also upon the excellent manner in which he has handled his estimates, particularly in view of the fact that this is the first occasion upon which he has had to pilot his estimates through the committee. I do not hand out compliments in any idle fashion, but in this instance they are well earned. The minister is in charge of one of the largest departments of government, a department having great importance and with tremendous ramifications. He has amply demonstrated that he is one of the most capable ministers to have occupied this portfolio. He has demonstrated an exhaustive grasp of his department and has certainly handled discussion in committee on his estimates with great skill. For similar reasons his deputy minister is to be congratulated. Hon. members are aware that the deputy minister came to the department only recently and he, too, has demonstrated a wonderful grasp of the work being done there.

I would appreciate knowing if any consideration is being given to the brief presented by the board of trade of Edson early in 1954 requesting that technical and financial assistance be given to improve the landing facilities at the airport at Edson. In the light of prevailing facts, however, I suggest this is a matter worthy of his consideration.
Edson is one of the most prolific oil producing areas in Canada. It is the largest town between Edmonton and Jasper and is the centre of an extensive air service serving the people of western Alberta and British Columbia. Any consideration that could be given to this subject would be appreciated.
Supply-Transport
No representations have been received recently but I shall be glad to have officials of the department look into the matter to see whether something ought to be done.

What assistance if any is given by the Department of Transport to municipalities in which airports are located? Does that include buildings?

Mr. Chairman, I have been making some investigations in connection with the airport at Revelstoke, and would make some comments in that connection at this time.
