Mr. Chairman, I should like to take advantage of the calling of this item to say a few words in relation to the over-all air policy, or lack of air policy, which we now see in this country. I was amazed this morning by what appeared to be the Jekyll and Hyde attitude of the government in this connection.
This morning the minister spent considerable time telling us about the unprecedented growth of air transport in this country. As a matter of fact, his vision this morning knew no bounds. This country was developing its air transportation by leaps and bounds, and I rather gathered it would be in the forefront in this connection in relation to its position with any other country in the world. The attitude seemed to be sharply in contrast with the answer which he gave last night in dealing with-and he may not agree with this terminology-or indicating the reasons for his interference in connection with probably the second most important case that has been heard in Canada in relation to competition between any of the major air companies.
Last night it was indicated that although the air transport board in its wisdom had recorded a decision in favour of an application covering a paralleling semi-scheduled line north of Edmonton into the Northwest Territories, the minister, without reading at all the evidence of the hearing, had decided in his wisdom that because of economic conditions in this country it was not an opportune time to grant such a competitive licence. This attitude, which was exemplified last fall in dealing with the economic conditions in the country, is strongly in contrast with the attitude of the government in almost every major debate in this House of Commons since the session opened. They said that everything was rosy in this country; there was no unemployment; there was nothing to worry about. A few short months before the session opened we were told that a competitive application was denied because of the economic conditions in this country. Then this morning we were advised that this country is in the forefront of air development and there appear to be no boundaries to where it can go. I should like to say that the people of this country are looking to the future with a vision that is apparently much broader in scope than that which is exemplified by the views from the treasury benches. Just how long are we going to have to wait for this position to materialize?

I notice in one of the Ottawa papers of June 17 of this year there is an indication that Trans-Canada Air Lines takes in more passenger traffic revenue than the Canadian National Railways. I should like to refer again to an editorial in the Globe and Mail of July 21, 1955, which deals with the situation which will develop as a result of the expansion of Malton airport. Part of the editorial reads as follows:
Protests were made at city council's meeting that Toronto should be declared an international airport. It is not a matter of simple declaration. For Toronto to become an international airport comparable with New York and Montreal, the countries and air lines concerned must make reciprocal agreements with the Canadian government. Such agreements are complicated-to put it mildly-by the fact that the Canadian government owns the T.C.A.
But the T.C.A. is getting on for 20 years old. It is surely strong enough by now to quit playing the role of dog in the manger, and to compete with other lines for European business emanating from Toronto. In fact, it is already doing so, since the majority of Torontonians make their European flights, not from Malton, but from Montreal or New York. Furthermore, T.C.A. would retain the advantage of its domestic monopoly. What more does it want?
With Malton airport firmly in Ottawa's possession, Toronto must now put pressure on Ottawa to provide it with more and better air service to and from Europe. The pressure will have to be strong, not only because Ottawa has a vested interest in T.C.A., but also because Ottawa is wary of taking, or seeming to take, anything from Montreal. Let our civic leaders, regardless of whether they voted for or against the Malton deal, unite with business and industry to get Toronto an air service worthy of the population it harbours, the traffic it creates, and the increasingly important place it occupies in the world.
These sentiments are echoed in an editorial which appeared in the Toronto Telegram of July 2, in which it says:
Malton may assume as inevitable its development as an international airport.
None of these things can be accomplished unless the lid placed on competition at the top in this field is removed. This is not the only place where this particular problem arises. We have the same situation in connection with trans-polar air service through Winnipeg. There is an opportunity to provide direct service to many thousands of travellers from the mid-west by the use of the trans-polar service which covers the area between Winnipeg and the European continent. Before that can be accomplished as well, we must have a change in the over-all policy.
What would competition do? Well, I read the other evening an excerpt from a news report from Vancouver. I referred at that time to the rejection of the C.P.A. air freight

application in connection with transcontinental air freight service. One of the things I did not read at that time is this additional item:
Rejection of C.P.A.'s air cargo application last November forced C.P.A. to revise plans for cargo rate reductions on its northern British Columbia routes. With integrated routes and the use of the two freighters, the company expected to cut freight rates in the north by 25 per cent.
Here is an indication that if competition were permitted at the highest level the benefits would be attained at the lowest level of private air service.
Mr. Chairman, there would appear to be a strong case for a revision of the government's position in this connection. At the same time I do not think it can be accomplished unless we remove interference from the air transport board.
I should like to read to you, Mr. Chairman, a short paragraph from the publication "Civil Air Policy", which is a report of the air co-ordinating committee under the direction of the President of the United States. It is dated May, 1954. Here are the recommendations of this committee and here is outlined the policy in connection with this business in the United States. On page 2 it says this:
In determining policies appropriate to air transportation, it must be kept in mind that this is an industry affected with a public interest. The responsibility of the government, however, is not to carve out some predetermined role for air transportation and then attempt to force the industry into such development. Rather, the government must provide a general background of sound regulatory and promotional policies within which the industry itself will have the greatest possible opportunity for finding its own proper mission in competition with all other forms of transportation.
Here appears to be a four-square formula to provide an adequate principle of expansion in this particular business. It will be accomplished only by a declaration of policy on the part of the government. It will be accomplished only by the provision of an air transport board free from any interference. It seems to me as well that it will be accomplished only if the government owned air line, from the standpoint of legislation, is placed on an equal footing with other bodies. I am wondering if the minister could give us any adequate explanation as to why after 20 years that particular government air line still remains outside the control of his department and is directed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce.

I would merely like to touch on one point. I think I said last night all I could say with regard to the subject of policy. With regard to the question of the S.A.S.
Supply-Transport
service from Winnipeg, I think that hon. members should realize that it is not a question of any T.C.A. monopoly that is concerned. I can see no reason why, and the officials of my department can see no reason why, we should grant traffic rights to the S.A.S. at Winnipeg unless we receive some privileges in return that we think are equally valuable.

Might I ask the minister if his department has made any efforts to see if he could obtain such reciprocal rights as he has referred to? What effort has he made to approach Scandinavian Airlines to see that those rights could be obtained?
All I can say in reply to that comment is that we can see no economic advantages at the present time that can be gained by an exchange with the Scandinavian countries.

but under the direction of the departmental officials. I am told that the same considerations with regard to safety apply to helicopters as to fixed wing aircraft. In reference to an emergency landing field in Ontario county close to the town of Beaverton, some time not long ago the chamber of commerce or the municipal authorities of Beaverton had some correspondence with your department. Beard of Transport Commissioners for Canada-
505. Administration, operation and maintenance, $996,540.

Mr. Chairman, I know I
should be considered derelict in my responsibility if I did not say a few words as a member from British Columbia on item 505, which deals with the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada. As we have a new Minister of Transport, I know I can say on behalf of all the residents of British Columbia that they hope it will result in a new approach and a new policy on the part of his department, the government and the board of transport commissioners, as far as freight rates are concerned, when dealing with the question of domestic grain moving westward into the province of British Columbia. I can very definitely say that all citizens in that province, all the city council, all the newspapers of British Columbia very strongly feel that that province has been grossly discriminated against in this matter
I Mr. Marler.]
of the freight rates on domestic grain moving from the prairie provinces into the province on the Pacific coast.
We all know that in the initial stages the capital cost of construction of railroads in that province must have been very heavy. There are four mountain ranges, we admit, but at the same time it should also be noted at the time of their construction all the railroads received invaluable assets in the way of grants of land and resources so as to assist them in the capital cost of construction.
I have heard it said that, of course, you have those four mountain ranges and so you have to pay more. However, if you go up a mountain one way, you go down it the other. It may be uphill one way, but it is downhill the other. If you make a study of the elevations from Calgary to Vancouver, it is downhill, and we are speaking about the transportation of grain to British Columbia on the downhill grade. We fail to understand why discrimination has been allowed all this time against the province of British Columbia. Just recently I received a memorandum containing a set of figures and information from a special committee in Vancouver operating under the jurisdiction of the city council of Vancouver. In it I note this statement:
There are two rail freight tariffs on grain and grain products from the prairie provinces to British Columbia points, (1) the export-or what is generally known as the Crowsnest rate-which is 20 cents per 100 pounds, or $4 per ton. (2) The domestic rail rate which is 54 cents per 100 pounds or $10.80 a ton.
We in British Columbia fail to understand why the citizens of that province are obliged to pay 170 per cent higher freight rates on grain utilized in our own province than those paid on grain if it is going to some foreign country and has to travel over exactly the same train route.
It is my understanding that on shipments of grain and grain products from the prairie provinces to the lakehead there is only one rail freight rate and that is the Crowsnest rate. If you study the domestic rail rate from Calgary to Vancouver-and that is a distance of 642 miles-you will find that the cost is 54 cents per 100 pounds. But if you study the domestic rail rate from Calgary to Port Arthur, which is a distance of 1,247 miles, you will find that it is only 26 cents per 100 pounds. If you work out the domestic rail rates on a per-ton per-mile basis, you will find that the Calgary-Vancouver rate is 1 [DOT] 682 cents per ton-mile as compared with the Calgary-lakehead rate-a distance of 1,247 miles-of 0-417 cents per ton-mile. You therefore see, Mr. Chairman, that as it works out on a per-ton per-mile basis, the people

of British Columbia are called upon to pay domestic rail rates on grain and grain products from Calgary that are 303 per cent higher than the Calgary-lakehead rate.
We fail to understand, on any basis of reasoning logic or justice, why for any longer period of time there should be this discrimination againt the people in the province of British Columbia. Surely we have now reached a time in our Canadian development when we should have an equalized system on the per-ton per-mile basis in this country. Surely we have reached the point where all citizens in all parts of the country should be treated on an equal basis. As a member from the province of British Columbia I strongly feel that I must express-as I am sure all other British Columbia members either have or will-the strongest protest. I am sure that the press of Vancouver, the people of British Columbia and the newspapers of British Columbia want to have expressed at this time the strongest possible protest against any further continuation of the discrimination. I want to ask the Minister of Transport if he will, at the earliest time, go thoroughly into this matter, if he has not already done so, take up the matter with the government and with the board of transport commissioners and remove this absolutely grave injustice to and discrimination against the people of the province of British Columbia.

I should like to ask the Minister of Transport what is the status of the arrangement made between the federal government, the province and the city of Halifax on the action being taken to correct the situation at the underpass at Fairview.

So far as the representations from Nova Scotia with respect to the Fairview railway

crossing are concerned, I should like to say that I had some representations made to me by the minister of highways and public works in Nova Scotia quite recently and 1 communicated the substance of those representations to the board. There is a matter which I believe was brought to the minister's attention on various occasions and through different channels. It is with regard to a very dangerous crossing in the constituency of Oxford known as the Creditville crossing. I was wondering whether the minister had any comment to make on that matter at this time.

First of all, I should like to thank the hon. member for having personally advised me of the situation at the Creditville crossing. He did so, I believe, on July 18. I immediately wrote to the chief commissioner and asked him for a report in connection with the matter. I should like to communicate to the committee the reply which I have received. It is addressed to me and reads as follows:

May I refer to your letter of July 18, 1955, concerning the further accidents which have occurred at the Creditville crossing. These further accidents, I must say at the outset, are in the same category as those earlier reported to you: that is to say, none of them have involved both a train movement and death or personal injury to a person using the crossing and were not therefore required to be reported to the board by the railway.
Perhaps hon. members will recall that the matter was discussed in the standing committee on railways and shipping. The letter continues:
You may recall that when this matter was first raised, full consideration was given to it by the board, although none of the accidents which had occurred in the vicinity were "crossing accidents" of the kind required to be reported to the board. The results of the board's inquiries and discussions were reported to you in my letter of May 2, 1955, and were, I understand, communicated by you to the railway committee.
Officials of the board have since then been in touch with the interested authorities at various levels: as recently as today it has been confirmed that the highway department has under advisement a re-alignment of the highway now crossing the railway, and a grade separation at the point at which the re-aligned highway will cross the railway. For your information, I am enclosing a copy of a letter and plan which were sent to the board by the department of highways, following a joint

I must add that the provincial department of highways has indicated that there are inherent difficulties in arranging for a re-alignment of a highway nearly a mile in length, particularly in view of the heavy property damage which would be involved, and I am informed that the cost of the re-alignment alone might well be in the neighbourhood of $250,000.

Mr. Chairman, I was very glad to hear the remarks made by the hon. member for Vancouver East a few moments ago. I heartily endorse every word he said. I was also interested in the reply of the minister, and I trust that the farmers of British Columbia and our citizens generally will be given every consideration in the matter of freight rates. There is another point I should like to take up at this moment in connection with the board of transport commissioners, and in order to put it more

clearly before the members of the committee I should like to read a short excerpt from a rather long letter I have here. The letter is from Mr. Charles E. S. Walls, secretary-manager of the British Columbia federation of agriculture, and reads in part as follows:
On June 14 a press release from Ottawa stated that the board of transport commissioners, in order to further equalize freight rates between eastern Canada and western Canada, was contemplating a 10 per cent increase in freight rates on domestic grain moving west, with an additional 10 per cent to be added in about a year's time. We understand this information was given off the cuff by the chairman of the board of transport commissioners following a meeting on June 13 dealing with equalization, a meeting attended by representatives of all provinces with the exception of British Columbia.
As there has since been no official notification of this freight hike on feed grain into B.C., this office wired the board of transport commissioners on June 27 asking for confirmation of the press release, as well as the date when it was contemplated that the increase would go into effect, and when appeals would be heard by interested parties against such a move. So far we have not received the courtesy of a reply.
We have heard about the high freight rates which we are already paying, and on top of this we have the threat of further increases. I am not going into the matter of freight rates at the present moment, but I believe there is something else contained in these short paragraphs that the minister should look into. I am greatly concerned about the arrogance-I know that is a strong word but I think it can be rightly applied in this case-of the board of transport commissioners in paying no attention to a telegram sent to them in good faith by this very reputable organization representing the farming industry of British Columbia. The possibility of freight rate increases on top of present discriminatory rates is a serious threat, and I think the farmers are entitled to know if this is likely to take place.
If the news release has no basis in fact, I feel that the board should lose no time in either denying the press report or replying to the telegram of the B.C. federation of agriculture. After all, the board of transport commissioners is a well paid body appointed to act as the servants of the people of Canada. As such it is their duty and is nothing more than common decency for them to reply to a telegram sent by an organization representing a large segment of the Canadian people. I suggest, therefore, that the minister should look into this matter and see that the board of transport commissioners gives courteous consideration to the request they have received from the B.C. federation of agriculture.

I am only going to be a minute. I had promised the farmers of my constituency that I would raise this question

and I simply rise to support the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver East. It is a matter of great concern to the farmers of British Columbia and I was very pleased to hear the minister's assurance that all interested parties would have a hearing before any action was taken.

I should like to draw to the attention of the minister the fact that during the past few years both the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National have been conducting quite an aggressive campaign to reduce services on the branch lines, and even at smaller points on some of the main lines in western Canada. They started out, first of all, by taking out the agents at the depots in the dry areas, but now they are going quite a bit farther and are making application to the board of transport commissioners to get these station agents removed from a number of points that have been doing quite well in the past and are doing just as well today. They are doing this at a number of points that could be considered to be really prosperous farm communities. It is true that the board of transport commissioners is not granting all their applications. They have turned a number of them down recently.
I am just wondering what the policy is going to be. I always understood that if there was a point where business was falling off and perhaps they were in the red, then they might consider taking out the agent. But I cannot understand why they would make application to remove the agent from prosperous farm districts. I could give a few examples in western Canada; there were Huxley and Rowley, both prosperous districts. Why would they try to get the agents removed from these points? It is true that so far the board has not granted their applications, but if they keep pressing for such action the

Supply-Transport
board of transport commissioners will eventually give way and remove these agents. If that action is carried out, it stands to reason the railways are going to lose a lot of business because the farmers will do more and more business with the trucks. It is true the railways say that the people can turn in telegrams at other points, but it is not merely a question of telegrams. In hot weather there is no suitable accommodation to look after cream shipments if the station is closed, and a great deal of inconvenience is caused.

I think I should say this, that the operating results of both the major railways last year have prompted the management in each case to examine every conceivable way by which economies in operation could be effected. I think it is an unfortunate fact that the only way in which economies can be effected in an operation of that kind is by cutting down the number of personnel. I am sure we all agree there are certain obvious limitations on how far one can go in that direction. When it comes down to branch lines and station agents at local points, I suppose it is a matter of examining the question from an economic viewpoint and deciding whether or not substantial economies can be realized.
I merely point out to the hon. member, as he has indicated, that this is not done except after ah application is made to the board, and the interests in the communities affected have an opportunity of making representations. The board is, I think, exercising a proper function in determining the arguments for and against those proposals, and deciding where the balance of inconvenience must rest.
I wonder if the minister could inform the committee if any applications have been received since the grade crossing fund was increased from $1 million to $5 million. If so, have any been granted?

Mr. Chairman, my interest in this item relates to a report of the board

of transport commissioners released this week permitting the discontinuance of the passenger service and the regular daily freight service on all lines in our province east and south of Charlottetown.
So far as the passenger service is concerned, although the ruling of the board will cause inconvenience, the fact remains that most people travel by motor car, and for those who do not own automobiles there is a compensating bus service.
But freight service is a vastly different matter. In fact we can say that freight service is the lifeblood of our agricultural province. I heard part of the hearing before the board of transport commissioners when I was home some time ago. Perhaps I should add in passing that I do not think the minister is in possession of all the facts because I have not had an opportunity to discuss it with him and it was only late yesterday that I got the details of the judgment. So in what I shall say, I am not implying any criticism of him.
At the hearing I attended I recall hearing counsel for the province suggesting to one of the chief railway witnesses that the discontinuance of the regular daily freight service in our province would constitute what he described as a disaster to our agricultural economy.
The railway had asked for permission to discontinue freight and passenger service on all lines west of Summerside and east and south of Charlottetown. The request concerning lines west of Summerside was denied. It is true that in their judgment the board of transport commissioners said that it would expect the railways to meet with shippers and the general public and try to arrange for a satisfactory freight service if possible. I think the gist of that statement hinges on the last two words, "if possible". I suppose the only procedure now is to await developments. But from what I heard there, and what I know personally about the situation, it is difficult to imagine a service such as was suggested being satisfactory.
I talked a few hours ago to the premier of the province by telephone, and outlined to him as best I could the details of the judgment as applied to freight. He had not seen the judgment, and his comments had to be reserved. However, he did agree with me that it seemed to him the arrangement would be most unsatisfactory, so far as freight was concerned.
I said a while ago that they granted permission to the railway to discontinue the service at one end of the province, but did not grant it in the other. So the judgment was perhaps a compromise. But compromises
Supply-Transport
are never satisfactory to all concerned. Speaking generally, this one most certainly does not appear to be satisfactory to the area in my province and my constituency which will be adversely affected.
I do not think I can be accused of twisted or biased thinking, because apart altogether from my own ability or desire to avoid such undesirable methods of approaching any situation, the fact is that about half my constituency is not affected by the ruling, although the other half is adversely affected.
Before leaving this matter there is one phase of the judgment to which I should like to call attention. Referring to the denial of the request to discontinue the passenger service on the line west of Summerside the judgment says:
This decision does not, however, preclude the railways from making adjustments in the passenger schedules on the lines in question or perhaps discontinuing some schedules. It merely prohibits the complete discontinuance of local passenger service on those lines.
I am sure that portion of the judgment will come as a surprise to people at home who are closer to this problem. In that connection I would refer to this further paragraph in the judgment:
Complaint was also made with respect to the type of passenger equipment used in Prince Edward Island, it being commented that one or more of the coaches presently in use are equipped with coal oil lamps and coal stoves and that if an improved passenger service were put into operation the railways might secure more passenger traffic.
We suggest that the railways give the above matter full consideration with a view towards providing better passenger equipment.
While in that paragraph the judgment contains the suggestion that a better passenger service should be provided, the paragraph I read earlier suggests that the railways are free to go ahead and reduce the service they are now giving.
My personal reaction to the discontinuance of the regular daily freight service, and the comments in this judgment, is that what is stated here does not recommend itself to me.
I am not going to weary the committee further. What I am saying may not have great point, in view of the fact that the minister has not had an opportunity to see the judgment-at least I do not believe he has-and certainly I have not had an opportunity to discuss it with him. But I did wish to register my protest on behalf of the people in my area who have been adversely affected.

Mr. Chairman, I was interested and somewhat encouraged to hear the minister's remarks because those of us on this side of the house are equally interested in the port of Montreal and some of us, such as myself, have a very particular interest in the port of Montreal. I am still somewhat perturbed at the lack of further information from the minister regarding these developmental plans of his. The reason for my perturbation is this. First, the amount provided for capital works in the port of Montreal this year is substantially similar to that which has been provided over the past two years. In 1953 there was provided $3,653,000; in 1954 there was provided $4,158,200; and this year there is provided $4,088,000; so that the amounts have been running approximately the same for the past three years. Therefore I suggest that any suggestion that the amount set aside for the port of Montreal this year indicates a rapidly expanding provision of the facilities there, or a large increase in the amount of funds made available for capital works in the port, is obviously untrue.
What is untrue?

The
statement that funds are being made available this year in excess of those formerly made available over the past three years for the port of Montreal. I have just buttressed that point with figures. In round figures in 1953 the amount was $3,600,000; in 1954, the amount was $4,150,000; in the present estimates the amount is $4,088,000. I suggest that

there is no increase whatsoever of an appreciable amount; in fact, there is a decrease from last year.
I would point out further to the minister that last year, according to the report of the national harbours board, $3,600,000 was spent on capital works in the port of Montreal. Certainly, therefore, to talk in terms of $4 million this year, or a total amount of $7 million, to carry the major impact of the changes made necessary by the St. Lawrence seaway and the growth of the port is most unreasonable. Furthermore, whilst the minister did indicate in very general terms that some additional amounts would be made available and there would be some additional work over and above that contemplated, I cannot find in his remarks any indication of a definite nature that these additional works will be provided. He says first, on page 6466 of Hansard:
It is proposed to make a start in the current year with the extension of two wharves, with the raising of the level of the Sutherland pier by 14 feet, the building of a new transit shed the extension of another transit shed and the carrying out of work on the grain conveyor galleries. The cost of these improvements I have just mentioned will be approximately $7 million.
That is his program set forth. In the next paragraph he says:
The later stages of the program to which I have just referred provide for the berthing and unloading facilities-
That is already covered, because he is extending the two wharves.
They have not been provided. They are additional, as I have explained.

the minister would give us the details in such a fashion that they could be understood by reasonable people on this side of the house, such as myself, we would get through this more quickly. Returning to the quotation: -required for the lakers, for the provision of more modern equipment for the handling of grain.
He has already provided for the carrying out of the work on the grain conveyor galleries. I suggest that these things are merely repeating what he already has provided. Let us not be asked to wait in this house until 1957 or 1958 for the minister to give us details of his over-all plan for the development of the port of Montreal in line with the seaway. That is what the seaway authorities themselves have done in connection with their work; they have kept everybody in the dark, and to a certain extent we are still in the dark. It has caused the city of Montreal great difficulty. Let us not have a similar situation in connection with the port of Montreal itself.

Let the minister come here and tell us in detail at this time, when it can be examined before it is necessary that the work be proceeded with immediately, what his plans are-if he has any plans-what his over-all plans are, exactly what facilities he proposes to provide and what works he proposes to undertake for the port of Montreal to deal with this situation.
The seaway is going to make tremendous changes to the port of Montreal. It is uneconomic that ocean-going vessels beyond a certain tonnage should use the seaway. That tonnage is usually set at 9,000. On the other hand, the lakers have a capacity of some 20,000 tons. Many experts foresee that transshipment of grain, iron ore and other commodities in the port of Montreal may grow tremendously. It is not sufficient for the satisfaction of those who are interested in Montreal to have these vague, general statements by the minister that he is starting some things this year and that they are going to cost $7 million, and then next year he is going to start some more things-he does not know what they will cost and he is not even sure what they will be, but trust the minister and everything will turn out all right.
Even in my short time in this house I have found out that that is a very unsatisfactory basis of operation and that it is wise to press for reasonable details and to obtain those details at the beginning of a project rather than having a situation similar to the most unfortunate experience the government has had with ports, with ships and I almost said "with ferries". I would not want there to be a recurrence of that situation in this particular instance. I hope the minister will rise and give us more adequate details.
While I am on my feet let me cover one or two other points referring specifically to the port of Montreal. First of all, the passenger-handling facilities in the port of Montreal have not been satisfactory for a number of years and they are growing steadily more unsatisfactory year by year because they have remained stationary while the volume of traffic and the comparable facilities elsewhere, particularly in the United States, have been improved.
I would point out to the minister that while the harbour of Quebec has had an increase in the passengers handled in that port from
74.000	in 1950 to 126,000 in 1946, the harbour of Montreal has had an increase only from
147.000	to 152,000; in other words, we are remaining almost stationary.
I suggest to the minister that one of the major reasons for that situation is inadequate and insufficient passenger-handling facilities

in the port of Montreal. I think that something should be done about that matter as one part of this program, and I think it should be done quickly because we are losing passenger traffic to the harbour of Quebec.
The other point that I would bring to his attention-and I brought it to the attention of his predecessor-is the need for a fire boat in the harbour of Montreal. I refer to a proper and adequate fire boat. The day well may come-though I hope it never does- when there will be concrete evidence of the necessity for adequate fire-fighting equipment from the waterside of the harbour. But if that day does come, people will die and property will be destroyed because of the lack of this particular fire-fighting equipment. Knowing the requirements of Montreal so well the minister might, perhaps, make that matter a point of discussion with the city authorities very quickly in order to iron out any difficulties and try to come to an agreement. Perhaps the minister will now give the committee more adequate information on what his plans are for the harbour of Montreal.

Mr. Chairman, I will deal with the last two points first. The hon. member complains about the fact that there is a drop in the number of passengers in Montreal, and I thought I understood him to say that there had been an increase in Quebec. I may be wrong. However, I do not really think it is material whether or not the situation is exactly as he has described it. I am sure everyone realizes that the situation, so far as the number of passengers arriving at a given point is concerned, is not determined solely by the facilities that are available there. I myself think that the terminals at Quebec are satisfactory; they are certainly quite modern. So far as the passenger-handling facilities in Montreal are concerned, this question of having a passenger terminal has been kicked around for quite a number of years now. The curious part of it is that those who do the kicking around are principally people who are not directly concerned with the movement of passengers by ships. The two principal lines which bring passengers to Montreal are opposed to the establishment of any passenger terminal in the harbour of Montreal and, so far as we understand it, are satisfied with the facilities which are now available for their ships.
On the subject of fire-fighting equipment may I say this. I can remember when the subject was brought up in municipal circles, not less than 14 years ago, that the city administration itself never felt that there was any need for it to participate in the purchase of equipment. I think it was the opinion of 50433-417

the fire department that, having regard to the length of the harbour of Montreal, the provision of a fire boat would be quite ineffective and that probably the fire would be over by the time the fire boat got there, if total destruction had not occurred in the meanwhile. Besides that, I might explain to hon. members who are not familiar with the Montreal situation that there is easy access from the landside to the harbour from one end to the other. The hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace seems to be taxing me and the government for the fact that we are not spending more money in Montreal this year. Nowhere in my remarks can I find anything in which I compared the expenditures of this year with those of last year. A moment ago I referred to last year's expenditures merely to explain a wrong figure that I had used in my remarks the other day. But I have not been comparing the expenditures of this year with those of last year. While I can readily understand that the hon. member would like to try to make out that we are doing less for the port of Montreal this year, because we have a few hundred thousand dollars less in the estimates this year than the total amount for last year, personally I am not at all convinced that that is a serious argument. I think what is really important, and what interests hon. members, the citizens of Montreal and those who wish to make use of the port facilities is what is going to be done.
I think I have said rather clearly what this is going to be. I have said that a supplementary estimate of $2,002,000 is the amount which will have to be spent this year for the first stage of a program which involves the expenditure of a total amount that is expected to be $7 million. That is $7 million for the first stage. From what I said a moment ago, I think what exactly was to be done with the $7 million was perfectly clear, and also exactly to what works the $2 million applied.
The hon. member seems to try to make out that I was asking the committee to have faith in the government and so on. No such words at all were ever expressed by me. I noticed throughout his remarks his main

Supply-Transport
argument seemed to be to put in my mouth words that I had not used and then proceed to show how foolish they were. May I say that it is a technique that I have seen used in other quarters, but that I do not propose to follow along those lines.
For the benefit of the hon. members of this committee who wish to understand, I am going to repeat that the program, in the first stage, contemplates the following works, and I will quote what I said in the house the other day as reported at page 6466 of Hansard:
It is proposed to make a start in the current year with the extension of two wharves, with the raising of the level of the Sutherland pier by 14 feet, the building of a new transit shed, the extension of another transit shed and the carrying out of work on the grain conveyor galleries.
I think there is nothing indefinite about that. I think it is perfectly clear and I think anyone acting in good faith will admit that it is clear. Given there is a picture of the works that are to be started this year. As I said a moment ago, the cost of these works is estimated to be $7 million and the amount which we shall have to spend in the current year is $2 million. There are other stages in the program, as I said earlier, and I want to make perfectly clear to all hon. members of the committee, including the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace, that the later stages of tne program do not embody any part of the first stage and that the works that are comprised in the later stages are not duplications of what is comprised in the first stage. The later stages of the program provide for the berthing and unloading facilities required for the lakers. I hope it is not my hon. friend's contention that we should do that long before the lakers are going to be there. Facilities will be provided for the time they are needed. They are not going to be provided at a time when they cannot be used.
I referred further to the provision of more modern equipment for the handling of grain. That does not refer to the same things that we are spending money for in the first stage of the program. There are other things to be done in connection with our grain unloading facilities and carrying out the work on the grain conveyor galleries. This is a more general expression of the work to be done because obviously it will be necessary to provide dredging for the widening of the channel and also dredging in order to provide access to two of the wharves. It will also be necessary to do other works and I said to hon. members, I thought very clearly, that I did not believe it would be desirable for me to outline in detail the proposed works that will have to be carried out between now and the time the seaway is opened because we
[Mr. Marler.3
are now approximately four years away, perhaps a little less than four years, and I did not wish to give the impression that the program is cut and dried, definite, settled and final.
The board has had a thorough examination made of the grain facilities in the port. They have considered most carefully the needs that will have to be met for the seaway and I think what I have said here, that "the later stages of the program provide for the berthing and unloading facilities required for the lakers, for the provision of more modern equipment for the handling of grain, and for the carrying out of such further work as will be needed when the seaway opens", is a very broad and clear description of the works that the harbour board proposes to carry out.
I should like to think that next year I would be able to get by with total expenditures of $4 million. I have no such hope whatever. I know that our expenditures in dollars in the next current year will be higher, and I suppose that we shall hear then from the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace that we are spending too much.

Let
me try to put this on as simple a basis as possible so that the minister will perhaps be able to give me a simple answer. When does the minister contemplate making public the details of existing plans for the over-all development of Montreal harbour in connection with the advent of the seaway so that interested parties may study these plans and make representations to the minister and so that he may have the benefit of advice and suggestions from all interested parties?
Just as soon as a final decision has been taken with respect to each part of the project it will be announced.

Mr. Chairman, I can see now that by trying to do the right thing around here you get yourself into a difficult spot. When the resolution was under consideration having to do with increasing the membership of the national harbours board, many hon. members who have local ports in their constituencies took the opportunity to make extended remarks, but I felt that was not the place to do so and I said I would make my big effort on the estimates of the department. When the first item of the department was under consideration I said no, that perhaps the proper place for extended remarks with respect to the national harbours board should be under that item.
So here we are today after a long weary session, and I imagine everybody is just as tired as I am. However, I am sure if I make a few brief remarks with respect to the

harbours board and the port of Saint John the minister will give them just as much attention as if I dragged my remarks out and presented a long story about our port and our new plans. In Saint John we have always had very good relations with the national harbours board, but of recent years we have realized that many mistakes have been made. Many of those mistakes are our responsibility, and in this respect I think we could have taken a lesson from Halifax.
In the 1920's the people of Halifax realized that port promotion was a big business. They set up some sort of advisory board and were perhaps able to co-operate a little better with the national harbours board in the development of that port. However, we have finally realized that it is big business and have taken the bull by the horns and set up the greater Saint John port and industrial commission with a commissioner who is experienced in the port promotion field. Recent figures have shown that the tonnage in and out of maritime ports has not been good for some time. In spite of the fact that the Minister of Trade and Commerce said the other evening that the maritime ports have received their greatest benefit so far as tonnage is concerned under a Liberal government in the last 12 months or more, I think that those who examine the reports of the national harbours board realize that this is not so.
Last year I referred to the 1953 figures of the board which indicated that both Halifax and Saint John had had decreases in their figures with respect to the arrivals of ships, the tonnage of those ships and the cargo tonnage. I will not refer to the figures in the latest report, which reviews the calendar year 1954, except to say that cargo business at eight ports showed a drop. I will admit that the 1955 figures for Saint John at least probably are much better owing to the increased movement of grain. However, I point out that the figures generally are not good for either Halifax or Saint John in recent times.
Coming to the main reason for my mentioning this situation today, I understand that it is the intention of the new expanded board to do more travelling throughout the country and to make a more detailed investigation of the problems of individual ports. As I say, in Saint John we have set up a commission headed by a man who is experienced in this field. We have called on the businessmen, the longshoremen, other union officials and everybody concerned with the promotion of the ports and the general welfare of the community. We hope that an effective liaison and co-ordination between businessmen and the national harbours board will result.

Finally, I should like to say that we feel we have a very fine old port. The longshoremen and other workers of Saint John have demonstrated during the war and in the post-war period that they can effectively handle any cargo coming to our port or going from our port. We do have misgivings about the seaway. We wonder whether the present plans for the promotion of Montreal and other ports on the seaway will mean a lessening of interest in those ports on which so much money has already been spent. We think that following the example of other ports and setting up a local advisory committee or port authority will help us in Saint John. When the resolution concerning the national harbours board was before the house I do not think the minister commented directly on the attitude of the department or the board with respect to these committees. Just how desirable are they, and to what extent should we go ahead with plans in this respect? Are we on the right track?
In closing, I should like to say that I understand a brief was presented to the national harbours board by this new group in Saint John. They have gone into these points extensively with the harbours board, and we have many local problems in connection with tides which have to be thoroughly investigated. I know the national harbours board will continue their good relations with us and will pay very strict attention to any suggestions we might make.

I would just add one word to that. If the interests in Saint John desire to organize an advisory committee for the port, I feel quite certain that they will find their relations with the national harbours board most harmonious. The board would be quite agreeable to receive any representations the advisory committee might care to make.

May I ask one further question, which is prompted by the remarks of the hon. member for Quebec West last night. I realize the minister touched on it in his first statement here today, with respect to the further plans for the development and improvement of Montreal and other ports on the seaway. Could the minister simply state the position of other ports, particularly Quebec and the maritime ports, in any future plans for expansion under the national harbours board?

I personally do not believe the position of Quebec, as one of the St. Lawrence ports, is going to be materially altered by the seaway. I think we will find the port of Quebec will carry on much the same kind of traffic, and under much the same conditions

Supply-Transport
as at present. We are making some substantial expenditures in Quebec in the coming year, among them a new oil berth at the Wolfe's Cove terminal on which it is expected to spend $1 million in the current year. There is some other work to be done which will involve a total expenditure of approximately $300,000 to $350,000.
I might say that I have personally asked the national harbours board to make a complete review of the present facilities in the port of Quebec, in order to ensure that the change in the type of shipping that is likely to occur when the seaway is opened does not leave Quebec in a position inferior to that which it occupies at the present time. More specifically, I understand at the present time there is no unloading accommodation at Quebec which would be suitable for lakers. If lakers are going to Montreal after the seaway is opened, I think they will also go to Quebec. I feel it will be necessary to provide facilities at Quebec in order that lakers can unload there. I do not want that taken as a commitment; that is an opinion of mine. I have asked the board to make a thorough review of the whole situation, so Quebec should not feel that it is, so to speak, on the end of the line and that its interests are going to be neglected.

It is interesting to observe that the minister has apparently settled the future of Canada's export grain trade, and has decided it is to be frozen according to his pattern. It may be that economic factors may not altogether agree with the minister's views on this matter. How does he know that lakers are going down to Montreal and Quebec? May it not be that ocean ships will go up to the head of the lakes? There may be good economic reasons why they should do so. Apparently all the minister's measures are predicated on the belief that the movement will be through the ports of Montreal and Quebec. I suggest it may be to the economic advantage of the grain producers in western Canada that their grain be handled for export at the head of the lakes rather than at either Montreal or Quebec.

I do not think the hon. member is being fair in suggesting that I was attempting to settle the future movement of grain in Canada, because nothing could be more absurd than that contention. It seems to me that anyone who has examined what has taken place in the past will find there is a more or less established pattern of movement. The pattern seems to have been to move grain from the lakehead to Prescott in the larger .ships, and to continue the movement from

Prescott to Montreal in the canallers. In Montreal it is transshipped into storage elevators.
When the ocean-going ships come to Montreal bringing goods and passengers they generally take back cargoes of grain to Europe. I do not believe the fact that it is going to be possible for ships of deeper draft to travel westward from Montreal into the great lakes is going to upset that long-established tradition. I am not settling anything, I am merely expressing an opinion. It is an opinion that is held not only by myself but by people who have had long experience in shipping, and long experience in the grain trade. I have found no one with any great familiarity with the subject who contended that the whole trend of the movement of shipping is going to be changed by the building of the St. Lawrence seaway. There obviously is going to be a great movement of shipping into the great lakes, but I think, Mr. Chairman, the economics are somewhat against the movement of larger ships into the great lakes in order to take on grain at the lakehead because the question arises of what are they going to carry to the lakehead?
Hon. members will say they are going to carry cargo, and of course there will be some movement. But I do not believe that the nature of the change is going to be so great that we are going to find a disruption of what I might call the traditional pattern. There are other persons much more qualified to speak authoritatively on the matter than I am who believe that the facilities provided for the traditional pattern should be extended and made ready to meet the change in domestic conditions that will take place as a result of the seaway.
The hon. member knows quite well that the lakers cannot get to Montreal now. When they do get to Montreal it will be necessary to accommodate them with longer wharves and with loading facilities that will operate much more rapidly than those now available. It is for that reason, and because it is in conformity with the traditional pattern, that it is necessary to make these expenditures.
The hon. member knows that it is not an easy thing for governments to change the habits of people. I think hon. members will agree that shipping goes where the cargoes are to be sent and where there is a need for service. Personally I believe we are going to see continued activity in the St. Lawrence. I think we are going to see a tremendous expansion of shipping in the St. Lawrence after the seaway is opened, and because of that fact I think we have to be prepared to meet the need.

Those are not the only expenditures that are contemplated by the national harbours board. As my hon. friend has probably observed, a further amount of $1,400,000 is being spent for a grain elevator extension at Churchill. We had occasion to talk about that yesterday. There is seemingly some promise of a growth of traffic into Hudson bay, and I hope it is going to continue. I hope Churchill will prove to be one of the great ports of Canada. Obviously these expenditures have to be made first in order to bring the ships there so those ships may have cargoes to take out.

If the minister is correct in his statement that all ocean freighters are not likely to come up to the lakehead, will there be much benefit to western farmers by way of a reduction in the cost of shipping grain?

My understanding of the situation is that there ought to be some not intangible benefits accruing to western farmers, because the movement of grain from the lake-head to Montreal, once the seaway has been built, will be accomplished much more economically than it is being done at the present time.
Just by way of illustration, at the moment you may have a laker which carries, let us say, 800,000 bushels of wheat from the lake-head to Prescott. I understand it will do so with a crew of perhaps 31 or 32. There it is transshipped into a canaller, which carries 80,000 bushels of wheat and a crew of 25 or 26 men. The canaller takes the grain from Prescott to Montreal. Obviously that operation is much more costly than the first one, because you have 25 men doing only a tenth of the work being done by 31. In addition to that there is the cost of transshipment at Prescott or to any other intermediate point, and the loading of the smaller canaller. So it seems to me quite evident that as between the one method we have at the present time of lakers plus canallers, and the other method of lakers only, which will be the case after the seaway is built, there ought to be very tangible benefits to the farmers. Everyone knows that the cost of transportation is not inordinate at the present time, but I have been told there is some possibility of a reduction of an extent that I think the farmers would consider worth while.
To follow the minister's argument to its logical conclusion, would it not seem desirable to eliminate the lakers and canallers altogether and load the grain directly on deep-sea ships?

If you are thinking only of shipment eastward from the lakehead, that
Supply-Transport
might possibly be so. But the distance between Montreal and the lakehead is very considerable. While I believe deep-sea shipping is going into the great lakes and probably up to the lakehead, I do not believe the economics favour deep-sea vessels going to the lakehead. I do not say none will go, but I do not think it will favour a large movement of that type of shipping, because I think that our domestic carriers are better able to handle domestic traffic moving by way of Montreal to the lakehead and from the lakehead to Montreal, and I doubt very much if deep-sea operators will be able to meet that kind of competition.

The minister's argument seems to be based upon the assumption that the centre of the continent is going to remain stationary, and not progress. I suggest that Chicago and the American middle west are going to be a big factor in this economic development, and it may be that western Canada will grow concomitantly.
That may well be.
I should like to ask about the port of Vancouver. In March, during the discussions on the national harbours board I raised the question of the local advisory committee for that port.
I think the hon. member first raised it in 1935, did he not?

Yes, it has been 20 years coming through, but it looks as if it will really happen now. I see from the Vancouver Province of July 16 that the city council has moved to set up an advisory committee in that port composed of 11 members, one of whom is to be the mayor and another an appointee of the Vancouver city council; then there are to be appointees from five other municipal councils, two from the merchants' exchange, one from the transportation bureau of the Vancouver board of trade and one from the predominant labour organization on the waterfront. Can the minister tell the committee whether the national harbours board has agreed to a committee of this kind, and whether there will be any difficulty in bringing about the utmost cooperation between the committee and not only the port manager but also the national harbours board itself?
I believe a committee of this kind can be of great benefit to the board and of even greater benefit to the city of Vancouver and the surrounding municipalities. What is the situation with respect to the committee at the present time?

My information is that the
city clerk of Vancouver asked the board

Supply-Transport
whether there would be any difficulty in connection with the organization of such an advisory committee, and the chairman of the board tells me the reply was given that no objection would be made by the board. I understand some efforts are now being made to organize an advisory committee in Vancouver, and I think I can say with respect to Vancouver that the remarks I made a moment ago concerning Saint John would apply equally to the western port.
Would the national harbours board agree to having a committee set up on the basis indicated in this article in the Vancouver Province?

Candidly, I do not think the board could express an opinion on a matter of that kind. That is a local question, and I think the board should deal with such advisory committee as the local interests see fit to establish. I do not think the board should do anything one way or another to control the kind of committee, the nominations, or any other part of it.

It seems to me this committee is well chosen. Then two or three years ago the government undertook to have a study made of the effect on the currents in Vancouver harbour of the dredging in the first narrows. A model was set up by the University of British Columbia, and it would be helpful if the minister could give us a report on the work done in this connection. I believe the dredging is practically completed. It was to be followed by further development work in the harbour, but that subsequent work was dependent on the result of these studies. Could the minister give a report of what has been accomplished?

The chairman of the board tells me a report has been made to it, and that it is currently under study. He tells me that the report is highly technical and I do not think he wishes to summarize its contents at the moment. Not having seen it, I am not able to add anything.

I believe my question would be in the field of the national harbours board, although it relates to an independent harbour commission. My question has to do with the relationship between independent harbour commissioners and the minister. My understanding is that they are required, under their incorporating act, to file an annual statement with the minister. Is that considered to be in the nature of a confidential report to the minister or, in effect, is it a public document?

My understanding is that the reports that are submitted to the minister are public reports which can be obtained from the independent harbour commissioners. If the 
hon. member is interested in any particular case he could without any difficulty obtain from the commissioners a copy of the report that is transmitted to the Minister of Transport.
A number of questions have been raised. They are public in the sense that they are available to any citizen of the country?
I think they are printed public reports in most instances, anyway.
Item agreed to.

545. Loans to the St. Lawrence seaway authority in such manner and subject to such terms and conditions as the governor in council may approve, $50,000,000.

Mr. Chairman, in connection with this item the minister suggested that I wait until this point to discuss the St. Lawrence seaway. Can we have a more adequate explanation of the expropriations being made in the Caughna-waga Indian reserve, the amount of land which is being expropriated, and why this is necessary beyond the immediate requirements of the seaway?

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say at once that there is no expropriation beyond the immediate requirement's of the seaway. The seaway is expropriating an area of approximately 1,250 acres. My information is that the strip of land is very irregular in depth, varying from a few feet to 4,500 feet at the eastern end. I am going to send a copy of the plan to my hon. friend and he will see, I believe, that the area to be expropriated lies particularly to the east of the Honore Mercier bridge. If the hon. member is familiar with the land in that neighbourhood he will recall that it is for the most part farm land and not the settled part of the reservation. At all events I assure him that it is not the intention of the seaway to expropriate in the reserve any more land than is actually needed for its purposes.

In
that connection I have in front of me not the latest but preliminary plans of land requirements in the Indian reserve. I think they will follow very closely the plans which the minister has in front of him. It is my understanding that in this area the route of the seaway follows very close to the shore line. In fact the seaway emerges from the land and enters lake St. Louis, I believe, at a point in the Indian reserve. The rough estimate I have made here, allowing some 600 feet in width-
The width is not uniform, as I said just a moment ago.

Excuse me; allowing some 600 feet in width for the seaway requirements-that is the point I am making. Perhaps I should show the minister how I arrive at this. May I quote from the report of the great lakes-St. Lawrence deep waterway made by the general engineering branch, Department of Transport, June, 1949, Guy A. Lindsay, engineer in charge. On page 1 we find navigation standards, which reads as follows:
The standards adopted for the proposed navigation improvement conform with those on the Welland ship canal. Navigation channels at 25 foot depth are to be not less than 200 feet wide on the bottom when flanked by two embankments; not less than 300 feet when flanked by one embankment; and not less than 450 feet when both sides are submerged.
Allowing for embankments on each side of a 200-foot channel and allowing in each case some 200 feet for such embankments, which is considerably more than the actual needs required; allowing the length of the seaway through the Indian reserve of some five miles, which again I think is overly generous, we find the total land requirement to be some
Supply-Transport
390 acres. The plans in the first place indicate that the expropriations are in excess of the requirements. Second, we find, as the minister has said, there is great variation in these expropriations. They have a tendency at some points to come right down to the river bank toward the end of the area and in others I think the minister said some 4,000 feet-
I said 4,500 feet.

-back from the river bank 4,500 feet. When one looks at the expropriation plans he finds that certain of this territory is far in excess of that required for the immediate needs of the seaway. Furthermore, Mr. Chairman, I would point out that the total expropriation of 1,250 acres is one-tenth of the total Indian reserve, the land area of which is 12,476 acres. It is a huge part, and includes some of the most valuable land in the reserve because it is almost completely waterfront land. Within that framework, can the minister satisfy the points I have raised?
