545. Loans to the St. Lawrence seaway authority in such manner and subject to such terms and conditions as the governor in council may approve, $50,000,000.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say with regard to this proposed expropriation in the Caughnawaga Indian reserve that the area of land to be expropriated for immediate needs is 1,250 acres, but as to a large part of that land the temporary use only is to be expropriated. The reason it is necessary to expropriate the larger area is not in order to find a site for the canal. Obviously the canal is not going to be located in this part of the reserve, but in order to carry out the construction operations efficiently it is necessary that there be space for men and

Supply-Transport
materials in connection with the actual construction operations. When that need is over the right of use so far as that part of the land is concerned is to be restored. I should not say it will be restored to the Indians, but the interest of the seaway will then be terminated in that part of the land expropriated.

think this is a rather interesting situation that has developed. I feel that the answer given to me by the minister when I first raised this question left one with the impression that this land was needed for the permanent use of the seaway. That was my impression. We now find that the greater part of this land is not needed for the permanent use of the seaway, but it is purely a temporary proposition. Yet I understand from the words of the minister that the seaway authority is going to move in and expropriate this land on exactly the same basis as that needed for permanent use by the seaway. Before I proceed, perhaps the minister would just nod his head that it is correct, that it is all going to be expropriated on the same basis.

No. I thought I had made that perfectly clear a moment ago. Actually, after the remarks of the hon. member, perhaps I should have said more fully that no expropriation plan has been filed in respect of the reserve. The extent of the land to be expropriated has been expressed in this figure of 1,250 acres. Discussions are going on between the seaway authority and the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. The exact details of the expropriation have not yet been worked out between the authority and the department, but it is not intended that there should be a permanent expropriation of the land to be occupied temporarily by the seaway authority's works. An additional area of land is to be expropriated for use only, and for use for a limited period.

May
I suggest most strongly to the minister that in a situation such as this where we are dealing with a group of people who have treaty rights to this land, who have been guaranteed by treaty sovereign rights to this territory in perpetuity, it is bad enough and inexcusable enough to expropriate the land that is needed for the permanent route of the seaway, but it is difficult to see any justification on any basis for the expropriation of land needed for only temporary purposes.
The abrogation of the Indians' treaty right to this land is causing them great concern, and quite rightly so. However, realizing the (Mr. Marler.]
great interests of this country and being willing to contribute to them, I think they will be prepared to agree eventually to the seaway channel crossing their land. But I do not see for a moment how the minister or anyone else can ask to expropriate land which is not needed for this final purpose. If it is necessary that the seaway have land in addition to that needed for its channel and the dikes on either side, let them negotiate with the band for the rental of it. Let them come to an agreement for the use of this land on a basis other than expropriation, but let them not move in and with all the power of the government simply take the land away from this band of Indians, use it and then throw it back at them again.
I would point out to the minister further that while he referred to farm land being expropriated, much of this area has major roads traversing it. Some of it has large numbers of homes on it. For these purposes there are people who are going to be dispossessed from houses which they have occupied for generations. To leave this band in the position where no differentiation is made between land which is needed for the seaway channel proper and land which is needed for ancillary purposes is a most unfair, unreasonable and unjust thing to do in so far as these Indians are concerned.
I cannot emphasize too strongly that we are dealing here not with people who are in ordinary tenure of land, but people who have a treaty with the sovereign of this nation and who have been guaranteed possession of this land and its occupation in perpetuity. When the government decides to abrogate that treaty they must have a vastly better reason than the one which has been given by the minister here this afternoon for the expropriation of better than 75 per cent of this land.
I would point out further, Mr. Chairman, that it is questionable whether this mass expropriation of land, this large area of land, is warranted. We have all seen construction work in process. I do not set myself up as an expert, although I have seen a fair amount of it. I know that on any construction job there will be construction roads, there will be parking spaces, there will be areas where stone crushers and various other facilities of that kind must be set up; but in relationship to a project of this kind the land required for these purposes will certainly not be as much as that which is going to be expropriated.
I would point out further that this route on the south side of the river is now chosen. There is nothing you can do about it. It is certainly one of two alternative routes. Here again we have the question whether it was

wise to choose this particular route in the light of the deprivations which must be endured by these people whose land the government has no right whatsoever to expropriate under any powers it may take to itself.
To sum up, Mr. Chairman, the original statement made by the minister gave us the impression, or at least it gave me the impression, that this land was needed for the seaway route itself. When one speaks of the immediate purpose of the seaway, one realizes that the immediate purpose is to construct the route of the seaway. When, by using documents obtained from our library here and by calculations one is able to make, it is possible to show in this house that the great proportion of this land to be expropriated is not needed for the seaway, the minister comes along and says it is needed for ancillary purposes. I point out to him that it is one-tenth of this reserve, that it is valuable waterfront land and that it is, in my opinion, far more than is needed for these purposes. I submit that a re-examination should be made of this situation and that the amount of land to be expropriated should be reduced substantially.

I think it would be just as well if hon. members of the committee knew the facts in connection with this proposed expropriation. I should merely say that so far as the permanent site of the seaway is concerned, it is in part passing through the settled part of Caughnawaga village. But as to the part in which it is proposed to expropriate merely a temporary right of use, my information is that the land is for the most part vacant and that there are few houses or buildings on the part which is to be expropriated in this temporary way.
If one knows the land itself, and if one appreciates the difficulties that are going to have to be met at this particular part of the seaway route, I think it will be appreciated that the seaway authority is not doing anything that is not necessary for its normal construction operations.
I	should just like to tell hon. members who are not familiar with the geography at this particular point in the St. Lawrence river that there is a railway bridge from which railway tracks emerge on the south shore of the river, with two branches; there are two highways, and there is a highway bridge leading both to the east and to the west. The difficulties of providing for the relocation of highway traffic alone are going to be considerable. When one knows the site one realizes how impossible it would be in the major part of this vacant land to allow the needs of a few occupants to complicate the construction operations. I should like to 50433-418
Supply-Transport
correct any impression that might be given to the committee that there was a wholesale evacuation of the Indians from land that was needed only temporarily. I think anyone who had such an impression would be misled, because that is not in conformity with the facts.
How many families are involved there? How many families will be involved in the expropriation of this land?

I am afraid I cannot tell the hon. member that, for this reason. As I said a moment ago the exact details of the expropriation have yet to be worked out between the seaway authority and the Department of Citizenship and Immigration.
I have one other question. Will not the building of the seaway require the raising at this point of the transSt. Lawrence bridge to allow an underpass of the highway?
It will. As a matter of fact it involves most complicated and most expensive operations.
It will require the taking of some land on account of the change in the curvature of the railroads coming off the bridge?
I think so; yes.

There are four brief questions I should like to ask the minister. First of all I may say I have the first annual report of the seaway authority, and it is a very interesting report. I was wondering if the authority had any estimates available-there are none given in the report-on the cost of such things as the Victoria bridge, the dikes, locks and that kind of thing. I was wondering if the seaway authority had any estimates of cost, in any detail; and if so, whether they could be made available to the members of the committee.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to avoid answering the hon. member's question; rather I want to give him the information he requires. I find it difficult to give him detailed information with regard to individual projects such as the Mercier bridge, the Victoria bridge or the harbour bridge.
If I might interrupt the minister-

I was going to suggest that perhaps I could give the hon. member the cost estimates of the seaway at present, as recently calculated, by the various sections in which the work is to be carried out. If that would be satisfactory, I would be glad to give that information to the committee.

Supply-Transport
In the Lachine section the cost estimated is $122,500,000; in the Soulanges section, $47,100,000; Lake St. Francis, $5,082,000; works at Cornwall, including head office building, $1,500,000; canal and lock at Iroquois, $15 million; deepening of Welland canal, $2 million; and contributions to be made to channel enlargement, $15 million. That makes a total of $208,182,000.

I appreciate that the minister would not have all that detail here. I was wondering whether at some future time, either before the end of the session or before the next session starts, the minister might have someone in the department prepare a breakdown of these figures in some more detail. I was wondering if that would be possible.

I have here three pages of details of these figures. If the hon. member is interested in any one of them. I should be glad to indicate it to him, but I hope he will spare me the necessity of giving three pages of details at this stage of the discussion.

I certainly do not want to ask the minister to take up the time of the committee at this stage to do that, but perhaps he could give them to me or other members at some future time.
The second question I should like to ask the minister is this. It is my understanding that the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys has prepared some studies of the St. Lawrence seaway. I understand that an employee of the department by the name of Camu has prepared some sort of study. If this is so, is that study available?

I have not heard of it, Mr. Chairman. Perhaps if my hon. friend would direct his question to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys when his estimates are before the house he might be able to answer that question.
I thought possibly the seaway estimate was the proper place to mention the matter.
I have not heard of it.

I thought the minister might nave it available. I have two other questions only, arising out of answers the minister gave to some questions I asked yesterday. First of all, it is my understanding that the deepening of the St. Clair river to conform with the 27 foot depth of the seaway is the responsibility of the government of the United States of America. Is the minister in a position to tell us whether or not the United States government has indicated to this

government, particularly the Department of Transport, if they intend to deepen the St. Clair channel, and when they intend to do it?

I would merely point out to my hon. friend, as I said yesterday, that in the first place the dredging in this part of the waterway has traditionally been done by the United States government, and that the existing channels are sufficient to enable the deep-draft vessels now operating in the great lakes to move up and down the river channels. Consequently I think it should be understood that there does not appear to be an urgent need for the carrying out of that work. I have not made a specific inquiry, but I have been told there is legislation pending before congress to authorize expenditures for this purpose. However, I do not wish to give the hon. member the impression that I have verified that fact.

Has the Department of Transport or the seaway authority made any specific recommendations to the Department of Public Works for the deepening of certain harbours on the great lakes and, if so, which harbours?
The answer to that question is no.

should like to say one more brief word on the seaway, and it is in the form of a suggestion to the minister. I think it would be helpful to all parts of Canada if a complete and authoritative economic study could be made as soon as possible of the seaway and its impact on Canadian trade, commerce and our economy generally. I am aware that the seaway authority has recently added to its staff an economist who, I believe, is doing some of this work. But we have had, particularly in connection with the seaway, specific instances where economic information of this kind has not been made available to the public. I refer specifically to the report prepared by the economic research division of the Department of Trade and Commerce in the winter of 1950-51. When a motion for the production of that report was moved in the house it was refused.
There is a great deal of comment, general discussion and opinion, some informed and some uninformed, on the economic effects of the seaway. To my knowledge there has never been a carefully documented and extensive study made of this subject which has been turned over to the public so that anyone interested could study it. I would recommend to the minister very definitely that such a study be undertaken in the immediate future, if it is not now under

way, and that once the results are obtained they be made available so we can all see them. They should not be hidden away in some government pigeonhole and cloaked in the secrecy in which much of the present economic information on the seaway is cloaked.

DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE Administration service-
1. Departmental administration, including advisory committee on agricultural services, $496,998.

Mr. Chairman, before the first item is passed there are a few observations about agriculture and the contribution that farmers and the department make in respect of Canada's economy that I should like to point out.
First of all I should like to compliment the minister, his parliamentary assistant and the department for the leadership and assistance that is given to all those engaged in agriculture in Canada. The 58-cent floor price on butter is a great help to the dairy industry, for it provides a base price to the creameries and concentrated milk factories and to dairy farmers across Canada. The minister is to be complimented on the security that is given to this basic production of a good food, butter.
Due to the extreme drought in Ontario farmers are now stable feeding their dairy cattle, using feeds that have normally been stored for next winter's use. The dry feeding period will be extended considerably and bring about added costs for feed and labour, and will decrease our milk supply. In this year's estimates you will find an amount of $400,000 to assist in the construction and reconstruction of cheese factories and the improvement of cheese maturing facilities. There is also an amount of $700,000 for premiums on high quality cheese. The floor price on hogs of 23 cents adds stability to the hog producers' market and goes a long way in assisting to provide steady deliveries of hogs to market. I also notice in the estimates that $5,660,000 will be paid to hog producers this year as premiums for dressed hogs, grades A and B, which go into first quality lean bacon.
The health of animals branch, at considerable expense to the department, assists us materially in keeping our animals in good health. All cattle are tested each year for tuberculosis. If any reactors are found they are slaughtered, with an inspector present, and the farmer is paid a reasonable amount for any animal destroyed. The test is almost 100 per cent accurate. The disease of tuberculosis is almost entirely wiped out, and the 50433-4181
Supply-Agriculture
health of Canadian citizens is protected through having milk that is safer to drink. This program also assists the sale of dairy cattle to the United States and other countries. The same government inspector, Dr. W. J. Drennan, has called at my home each year beginning with 1923. Calfhood vaccination also gives material assistance in ridding cattle of Bang's disease.
Class A and B fairs receive grants of $270,000, an increase from the amount of $222,000 paid in the previous year. Incidentally, Norfolk has one of the best fairs in Ontario. An amount of $420,000 is also to be given to fair boards for the construction of necessary buildings. Freight assistance on western feed grain to farmers in the east will amount to $151 million. The livestock production service costs the department over a million dollars each year, and salaries paid to record of performance inspectors amount to almost half a million dollars.
These inspectors call at our homes about once each month, weigh the milk for one day, take samples and test the milk. The R.O.P. certificates issued at the end of the year give progressive farmers the opportunity to develop better strains of dairy cows and weed out the poor ones. The inspectors live in the farmers' homes for one day. They are a very good type of men. They are screened for the work they do, and are able to give farmers valuable advice.
Right here, Mr. Chairman, I want to pay a tribute to all the inspectors who have called at my home and tested my cattle since 1919. I could cite many more instances where the department gives valuable assistance to aggressive farmers who have the ambition to improve their herds and better their own position, but I shall leave the matter there.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I have a request to make of the minister. The income of farmers is not as favourable as it has been in previous years. Our cost of production is at the same high level as in former years, and in some cases higher, so if farmers are to maintain the same standard of living they will have to be very efficient. I can think of no better way for the department to assist us than to erect and maintain, with a suitable staff of trained technicians, an experimental station in Norfolk which would serve Norfolk and the surrounding districts. The provincial stations give us all the help they possibly can, but their own work is increasing and we need a dominion station in that area. I believe, subject to correction, that our nearest station is at Harrow in Essex county. There is another one at Smithfield near Trenton in eastern Ontario, but a station in Norfolk could serve all of central Ontario.

Supply-Agriculture
This house will appreciate the fact that a large number of Norfolk's good farmers were born in other countries, but they will respond as quickly as anyone who has always lived here to anything that will advance their position. We have a tobacco substation at Delhi under the management of Mr. Vickery, and it has assisted tobacco farmers. The station has given us new, improved varieties that can be harvested earlier in the year, thus lessening the danger from frost. Tobacco growing is the source of our major grower income in the district, and I am told that the tobacco farmers in Norfolk and surrounding districts were paid $67 million in 1954 for flue-cured tobacco. I would hope their expenses would be somewhat less than that, but it is a definite fact that flue-cured tobacco is a very expensive crop to grow.
We need assistance and leadership in many fields. One new field is irrigation, and there were many miles of irrigation pipe laid in 1954. In this dry year of 1955 irrigation systems are being constructed by the hundreds. These systems are new in the district, and the farmers need advice.
I should like now to give the committee some of the production figures for Norfolk county for 1954. The figures wefe prepared by the dominion inspection service. More fruit is grown in Norfolk than these figures would indicate, because they do not take into consideration the quarter acres and half acres of all the people who grow fruit and take it to the surrounding markets.
In this county we have 2,000 acres of apples and in 1954 there were 395,000 bushels produced. Apple plantings are on the increase and one grower, Bruce Wallace, has 67 acres just starting to bear. There are 30 acres of sweet cherries, which produced 640 bushels. There are 142 acres of sour cherries which produced 16,730 bushels. We have some grapes, and last year we produced 90 tons. This could be expanded. We have the land and we have the climate there, so we could grow a lot more grapes. There are 495 acres of peaches which produced 62,885 bushels. There are 66 acres of Bartlett pears which produced 20,000 bushels. There are 103 acres of Keifer pears which produced 16,000 bushels. There are only about 50 acres of plums, but they produced 11,000 bushels. The raspberries were low, and 65 acres produced only 101,000 quarts. We had 1,100 acres of strawberries in 1954 which produced 3,300,000 quarts. I am not sure of the number of acres of strawberries in 1955, but the production was 5 million quarts. Plantings are increasing. One grower in Norfolk, John Cooper, sold 3 million plants this year and the county sale would run to about 1 billion 
plants. We need new varieties. We need help to fight virus diseases such as leaf roller and other new diseases such as June yellows that are appearing each growing season in strawberry plantations. Norfolk county and district also need direction in the sharp freezing of fruits and vegetables. We must also have advice as to the best varieties to freeze.
Then, Mr. Chairman, I should like to put on the record the vegetable production of Norfolk county. The following table gives
the production:	Acreage	ProductionTomatoes, fresh market	100	15,000 bushelsAsparagus 	125	139 tonsCabbage 	120	1,040 tonsCauliflower 	50	15,000 dozenPotatoes 	1,190	175,000 bushelsRutabagas 	100 tonsSweet corn for table use 	3,000	450,000 crates
I am not sure how many ears of corn are in a crate, but there are five or six dozen. There are 48,000 square feet of mushrooms in the county, which produce 71 tons. In addition to the items listed above there is a considerable acreage of tomatoes, corn and peas for canning, and a small acreage of such crops as carrots, beets, cabbage and cauliflower. There would be some hundreds of tons of tomatoes, corn and peas produced each year for canning. If it were possible for the department to give the county of Norfolk an experimental station these production figures could be increased, perhaps doubled in some cases. We have the land and we have ambitious people who will carry out any program under proper direction.
Then, too, one must consider the industrial and residential expansion in the areas along lake Ontario from Niagara Falls to Whitby, Clarkson and elsewhere in Ontario. As a result of this there will be an increased demand for land suitable for the production of many of our fruit and vegetable crops. Norfolk county and district has this land, but we feel there is a great need for more leadership and experimental work in developing varieties most suited to this area. We feel there is a big field of service open in this district of Norfolk, and an experimental station there would improve our economy and be of great benefit to the Canadian welfare.

First of all I must congratulate the parliamentary assistant upon having the opportunity to pilot these estimates through the house. I hope he has an enjoyable time before they pass tomorrow night. I rise particularly because I have been faced with a problem that has not been solved to date. Before I came down here I had several

of my consumer constituents who wanted me to find out when a lamb became a sheep. I was able to direct my inquiry to the summit, the summit being the Minister of Agriculture.
I asked him that question and I was very much surprised when he said he did not know. As a matter of fact, from my point of view the infallibility of the Minister of Agriculture foundered on that woolly question.
He was pulling the wool over your eyes.

However, since that time I have been anxious to get the facts, and have inquired from three different departments of government. I am still in the dark. I wrote a letter, to which the parliamentary assistant kindly replied by stating:
Lamb and mutton are defined in the regulations under the Livestock and Livestock Products Act 1939 and P.C. 4932. The specifications as defined are as follows:
"lamb carcass" means the carcass from an animal of the ovine species, of either sex, up to approximately twelve months of age, having four well defined, relatively soft ridges at the break joint of the forelegs.
"mutton carcass" means the carcass from an animal of the ovine species, of either sex, being approximately twelve months of age, or more, having two smooth hard white ridges where the feet are severed at the ankle (spool) joint, and bones somewhat whiter and harder than those in lamb carcasses.
There is nothing in the regulations to make it obligatory that anyone is required to mark or identify lamb or mutton as defined in these regulations.
Then I wrote another letter to the Department of National Health and Welfare to which I received this reply:
For purposes of record, the health of animals division of the Department of Agriculture classifies sheep that are less than four months old when slaughtered as lambs. Animals younger than three weeks are considered as immature and are not slaughtered for food.
Then I inquired of the Department of Transport, and that department told me that so far as they are concerned all lambs are sheep. So I have not had my question answered yet. I would like to get the facts, because a number of my constituents who are housewives are interested in this question. They are of the opinion that they are buying a lot of lamb that should more properly be sold as mutton or sheep. Can the parliamentary assistant give me the correct answer to what apparently is a mystery?

I should like to ask the parliamentary assistant some questions in connection with the New Brunswick potato marketing board. Back in 1953-54 the prices support board undertook to support the price of potatoes, and there is some settling up that has not yet been completed. I understand now, however, that the operations have
Supply-Agriculture
been completed by the R.C.M.P., and I should like to know when we might expect the report to be filed.
I would ask, further, how much money was authorized for expenditure by the treasury board under the Agricultural Products Cooperative Marketing Act? What proportion of the amount authorized covers support to the growers? How much money went to the growers of the potatoes and how much was used in paying salaries to officials of the board and field men by way of expenses? If the parliamentary assistant cannot give a reply now, perhaps he could give the information later.
Then I have another question in connection with certified seed potatoes, a matter which is of considerable importance in my province and in Prince Edward Island. I am not sure whether the question should be asked now or later.

I should like to mention a matter which it seems to me would be appropriate at the moment, namely that of giving assistance to those in Ontario who are suffering from drought at the present time. We in Alberta and Saskatchewan have had so much experience with drought that we are accustomed to taking it in our stride, and being in some measure rewarded for our losses. I am wondering if some provision is being made by the department at this time to bring to the people around this district who are losing their crops as a result of drought some relief by way of something like a temporary application of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. If something like that is not being contemplated may I suggest that it be undertaken at once, so the farmers in this area who are suffering seriously may receive some encouragement.
Next may I comment on a matter to which the whole country should be giving thought,

Supply-Agriculture
namely the rapidly increasing cost to farmers of doing business. A recent survey in the United States shows that in 1940 the average investment per agricultural worker for all farms in the United States by way of machinery and other requirements was $3,500, while in 1955 it has risen to $14,000. This means that within those 14 years the cost of equipment has become four times as great. Unless the thinking of the country as a whole, including not only the cabinet and the Minister of Agriculture but every political party, is adjusted to meet that tremendous increase in the cost of doing business in agriculture, then we shall have a serious mismanagement of our farming population in respect of prices and other considerations.
Someone may say, "We do not want special considerations for farmers." That is an entirely fallacious attitude. Farmers are not just ordinary citizens; they are people who are engaged in the production of food, and they are in the grip of serious economic changes. The farmer on the land is just as important as is the man engaged in any other gainful occupation in Canada. His prosperity and his ultimate financial success are just as important to the nation as is the success of any person else in Canada. We must make provision to see to it that he has the additional assistance he needs, not because of any fault in himself but because of the rapid onrush of machinery and the high costs of implements of various kinds.
The same investigation in the United States indicated that the amount for buildings which was necessary per worker at the present time was $5,000, making a total of $19,000 for the average worker on farms in the United States. On an average winter wheat farm-now we are getting into trade and commerce, I know, but we cannot keep them entirely separate-in the United States northwest, the investment is about $70,000 per worker. The average cash grain farm in the cornbelt has $60,000 invested per worker. The average value of the equipment at the disposal of each farm worker in 1949 was little more than $200. In 1955 it is $1,900.
I do not wish to spend any time commenting on that situation any further, except just to bring it to the attention of the minister and the committee so we can be rather generous in our consideration of the problems of the Canadian farmer.

Mr. Chairman, I have been interested in listening to the various hon. members participating in the agricultural debates during the session, and also on the first item when it came before us some days ago. I noted with interest the exchanges that
[Mr. Blackmore.l
passed between a member from the western provinces and a member from the eastern section. The member from the eastern section thought the western members felt that all the farming that was carried on in Canada was conducted in the prairie provinces. I should like to say that not only is farming carried on in the prairie provinces and in the eastern provinces of the country, but also in British Columbia to the west of the Rocky mountains.
I should like to refer to the agricultural activities of my own particular riding, because I feel that in a way they have been pushed somewhat into the background mainly through the discussion of the wheat situation in Canada at the present time. I know we are all in agreement with the suggestion that agriculture is an industry of primary importance to the economy of Canada, and that the welfare of our nation is to a large degree dependent upon the welfare of our agricultural population. Because of that fact I feel that we have before us now the estimates of one of the most important departments of government, as they affect the industry that is perhaps closest to the people as a whole and is the vital concern of every one of us.
In referring to agriculture, as I have intimated, I am not speaking or thinking of the great fields of grain, or the granaries and elevators that are bulging with unsold grain. I propose to leave that to the members who represent the areas where that situation obtains. I have the privilege and honour to represent one of the great agricultural areas of the province of British Columbia, namely the Fraser valley. There are, of course, other activities there as well, but a great number of our people are dependent upon income from agricultural operations, and certainly its continued promotion is essential to the welfare of our particular community. Dairy farming occupies the attention and energies of a considerable number in my riding, and of course dairy farming is one of the leading operations in the agricultural field in Canada as a whole.
I hold in my hand "Dairy Facts", released by the office of the national dairy council of Canada, in which it is stated that the dairy products processed at the factories and milk plants had a value of $700 million; the value of livestock sold from dairy herds, $125 million; and the value of farm-made dairy products, $75 million, which gives the gross value of the Canadian dairy industry in 1954 of $900 million.
That has a very great effect upon the economy of our country, when we think of it not only from the economic point of view,

but also from the point of view that it is so necessary to the health of our nation. In a pamphlet that was issued a short time ago it was stated that 20 cents out of every dollar spent on food are spent for dairy products, and for that 20 cents the housewife gets more than one-third of the nutrients with which she feeds her family. Therefore we may say that from the health point of view, agriculture and the dairy industry do have a vital effect upon our people.
A look at the statistics-and I shall not take the time of the committee to quote them-will show that the Fraser valley is making a valuable contribution to this phase of the agricultural industry.

Mr. Chairman, just before the committee recessed for dinner I was emphasizing the importance of the agricultural activities of the Fraser Valley constituency which I have the privilege and honour of representing. Respecting the economic status of dairying in that particular area, Dr. Mills Clarke, superintendent of the dominion experimental farm at Agassiz, speaking to the Chilliwack rotary club some time ago, stated that the dairy industry remains the most important single source of income in the valley.
Not only would I like to emphasize the fact that revenue comes to the farmers from this
Supply-Agriculture
industry; I should also like to emphasize the quality of the product that is sent out from the Fraser valley. I have here a copy of an article from the Hope Standard dated February 23, 1955, which reads as follows;
In Canada during the 12 months ending November 27, 1954, there were 44,072 boxes of butter graded "94" the top grade. Out of this figure, 40,064 boxes or 90-9 per cent was made in the Sardis utility plant of the Fraser Valley milk producers' association.
A box of butter contains 56 pounds. Thus nearly two and a quarter million pounds of butter made from the milk of Fraser valley dairy cows was rated in the "best'' category.
Of the total butter make of the F.V.M.P.A. over 5,400,000 pounds in 1954, 95 per cent was Canada first grade creamery butter.
I just wanted to put in that plug for the Fraser valley and for the quality of the dairy products that are placed on the market from that area.
There has been considerable debate on the matter of subsidies or support prices for butter. I think at the present time and under present conditions this is vital and essential. Mr. Gilbert McMillan, president of the dairy farmers of Canada, has said, and I quote from an editorial in the Montreal Gazette of Friday, June 3:
"Wreck the price of butter and you wreck the dairy industry. Without a floor price on butter, the industry will have no stability."
This editorial continues:
A similar view has been expressed by H. J. MacDonald, dairy superintendent of the agriculture department of Prince Edward Island. He says that if the federal government gave up its price supports on butter, the whole dairy industry would topple.
I know there is considerable discussion relative to the value of those support prices and whether butter should be supported in this way. In the Ottawa Citizen of June 1 [DOT]there was an editorial with the heading "The Butter Support Program". In part the editorial reads as follows:
The butter support program, which began about the time margarine appeared, is in its seventh year. Up to the end of March it had cost the treasury about $3 million. To this must be added the still undetermined cost of disposing of the present surplus. When the total bill is in, it will be interesting to compare it with a single year's subsidy to the coal industry (roughly $10 million) or to gold producers ($16 million). So far, at any rate, there is nothing to warrant views that the price of keeping a relatively stable butter market in Canada since 1949, in the combined interests of producers and consumers, has been extravagantly high.
So, Mr. Chairman, we recognize the importance and necessity of support prices.
The problem of disposing of the butter surplus at the present time is still very vital. Various suggestions have been made. Some days ago the hon. member for Acadia suggested one way in which something could be done in this connection. He suggested

S upply-A griculture
the use of a stamp program whereby those who are receiving allowances and pensions could obtain stamps enabling them to buy extra butter when they make regular purchases of that commodity. I think that is a very good suggestion which should be considered by the government.
So, Mr. Chairman, this shows that in the Fraser valley dairy farming is very important and very vital, and the Fraser valley is making its contribution to the economy of Canada in this particular respect.
There are just two or three other matters to which I wish to refer in connection with agricultural activities. We are in one of the best berry growing sections of the province, and I may say of the country. According to figures published by the dominion bureau of statistics the production of strawberries and raspberries for the years 1953 and 1954 was as follows. In 1953 the production of strawberries was 12,425,000 quarts, with a farm value of $2,716,000. In 1954 the production was 8,408,000 quarts, with a farm value of $2,531,000. In 1953 the raspberry production was 8,929,000 quarts, with a farm value of $1,702,000. In 1954 the production was 9,024,000 quarts, with a farm value of $1,791,000. I may say that of these quantities a substantial part is grown in the Fraser valley. These figures will indicate the importance of that industry in our area.
I do not know whether or not the estimates of production for this year are going to hold up, on account of the unsatisfactory climatic conditions. There is apparently a considerable reduction in the production of strawberries, but the estimates were in the neighbourhood of 7,500 tons of strawberries, and 7,000 tons of raspberries. That is a lot of berries. But they are facing some very serious problems. There is in the valley great concern over the local strawberry crop of 2 to 2J tons per acre having to compete with strawberries grown in Oregon at the rate of from 3i to 7 tons per acre and those grown in California at a rate ranging from 12 to over 20 tons per acre. We thus see that they are faced with an extremely serious problem in that regard.
Then there are other factors that enter into the problems they are facing. They have had considerable difficulty with insects, and experiments are continuing in an endeavour to find some practical way in which to deal with these particular weevils or insects that are causing great loss to the strawberry growers.
One of the other problems they are facing is that of decreasing production per acre. They have more or less concentrated on one particular variety, namely the Sovereign. Other 
varieties are now being tested. These experiments have been carried on at the experimental farm in Agassiz. I may say that this experimental farm is making a worth-while and valuable contribution to the farming economy in that area. I am sure that all those in that section are appreciative of the co-operation that is being given by that particular farm. They are continuing with the studies and surveys in an endeavour to bring up production and also reduce the cost of production in order to compete with berries from these other sections. We can therefore see that there is a real necessity for maintaining and developing a ready home and export market for the encouragement and development of that vital industry.
There are, of course, other activities. We have an extensive vegetable production. Peas, corn, beans and so on are produced there and they are canned right in the area at the various canneries.
I should just like to say a word about the poultry industry. I would point out that 80 per cent of the poultry industry of British Columbia is located on the lower mainland. Tying this fact in with the other sections of the farming community that must purchase the feed grains that are shipped into the province of British Columbia, I should like to refer again to the freight rate assistance which has been paid in the past but which has been drastically reduced, and then to refer to the rumoured increase in freight rates. Some of that material was placed on the record this afternoon in another debate, but I should just like to read one section of a letter dated July 7 which I received from the British Columbia federation of agriculture. I shall read just this one paragraph:
British Columbia livestock and poultry feeders have already been hard hit this year by the reduction of $5 per ton on the government's freight assistance subsidy covering feed grain moving into this province and it should be realized how serious the additional increase in freights would be when we draw to your attention that the 1954 dominion bureau of statistics figures just released show that the maritimes only have to spend 22 per cent of the income they receive from livestock, dairying and poultry towards the purchase of feed grain whereas British Columbia has to spend 35 per cent] and the across Canada average is only 19 per cent! The two contemplated 10 per cent freight rate increases will add another half a million dollars to our poultry and livestock men's feed bills.
Hence we see how these decisions affect in such a drastic manner the activities of the farmers in the Fraser valley and in British Columbia generally. As has been emphasized by other members this afternoon, I certainly feel that every consideration should be given to working out some plan whereby those farmers will receive the necessary protection

and assistance so they can carry on their activities in connection with farming.
I just wanted to place on record again at this time the fact that there is farming west of the Rocky mountains. It is not all carried on on the prairies, in Ontario or farther east. We in British Columbia have an extremely valuable agricultural industry. We want to do everything we can, and we want the department to do everything it can, to assist in the continued development of that industry.

I have just a few remarks to make at this time, Mr. Chairman. Item No. 1 was before the house when the Minister of Agriculture was here, and it has been fairly well discussed. I want to wish the parliamentary assistant well in his new office and to express the hope that we can facilitate the passing of the estimates. We shall be glad to do so in any way we can. Before we go into that matter, however, I should like to point out to him what I consider to be a most serious defect in the agricultural industry in Canada today.
The hon. member who has just spoken has referred to the fine farming facilities and the production in the Fraser valley. The dairy industry across Canada is one of the big industries, and it probably affects more parts of Canada than does any other single production factor in the whole of agriculture. It is for that reason that we have always supported a floor-a parity price, as it were- under butter, and we have been pleased that the government saw fit to take this action. When the Department of Agriculture did that, they gave stability to the dairy industry. But they seem to have stopped there. I think what I have to say tonight will point up the need for carrying on that price support program into other fields if the agricultural producers in other parts of Canada are not to continue to suffer a decline such as that which they have suffered in the past few years.
There is something seriously wrong with agriculture in a country which has only about 20 per cent of its population engaged in making their living in that industry. The reduction in the percentage of people engaged in agriculture in Canada is a sign of that decline. Just 24 years ago a large number of Canadian people were engaged in agriculture; I think the percentage was as high as 37 per cent. Perhaps the fact that today our percentage is down to 20 per cent is an indication that the people are leaving the farms and leaving agricultural life.
Of course it is true that agricultural production is more efficient today. We farm with machinery. No one would recommend that we should go back to the old horse and buggy
Sup p ly-A griculture
days or the use of oxen, which we still find in some parts of Canada. But it is good for the economy of any country and for the standards of citizenship that people be engaged in agriculture and make their living in that way. The strength of a nation as well as of its people comes from the agricultural areas. Agriculture is too important to any nation for it to be allowed to stagnate and decline.
Bureau of statistics figures reveal a situation which I think is one to cause alarm, namely that the 20 per cent of our people who are engaged in agriculture last year only got 9 per cent of the national income. If these figures are correct it means that those who are making their living from farming are not getting half as much as they should. If they were getting their fair share they would have 20 per cent of the national income, and they are only getting 9 per cent.
How can this situation be improved? As the minister knows very well, a large portion of Canada's cash farm income comes from the sale of wheat, and the crop failure last year affected the prairie producers rather seriously. Figures of the Department of Agriculture show that the net income of the average farmer in Saskatchewan was reduced 70 per cent last year. The rust which affected the crop last year is one of the hazards of the occupation of farming, and the farmers were hit very severely. They are in a very difficult position.
The Minister of Agriculture is very fond of getting up and saying how much money the farmer received last year, that he never got so much money in his life and would not want to go back to the days of the thirties. Of course not; but the minister ignores one very important part of the farming picture today, the farmer's costs of production. It is in this field that farmers have been squeezed the most. Costs of production are constantly and rapidly increasing, and the farmer has no control over them. The causes of the increasing cost of production go back to the policy of the government of allowing the cost of living to increase. In the past 14 years the cost of living has increased about 100 per cent, which means that the wage earner, the worker in the factory, has had to seek more money. That has been the cause of strikes on the part of workers to get more money in order to meet the higher costs of living. The costs of living continue to rise, the costs of labour continue to rise and the costs of everything else involved in the carrying on of industry are going up. The result is that the manufacturer must charge more for his product.

Supply-Agriculture
I believe the greatest mistake the government ever made so far as the Canadian people are concerned was in doing away with price controls and allowing the cost of living to rise, with no redress for those who want to sell their higher priced commodities in the markets of the world. When the Minister of Trade and Commerce was discussing his estimates the other day I asked why the Canadian farmer had lost his market in Britain. I asked why we cannot get back our market in Britain for bacon and beef. The minister said if I knew of any farmers who wanted to ship their cattle and hogs to Britain at the prices they would get there he would be very glad to know about it and they could ship them. Of course he would, but it is the fault of the government that costs are so high. It does not pay people to raise hogs at 23 cents a pound dressed or to market beef at the prices being paid on the prairies these days.
The government took away from the prairie producer the opportunity to make extra money through the production of hogs and livestock in a year when his grain crop was affected by rust. If the farmer could find a market for his production in the same quantities we sold a few years ago, when we were shipping hundreds of tons of bacon to Europe, then a crop failure brought about by rust would not bother him. The farmer cannot continue to produce hogs at 23 cents a pound for No. 1 grade, basis Toronto, at today's costs of production. Therefore if there is going to be stability in any part of farming other than the dairy industry, support prices must be placed under livestock products to encourage the farmers to engage in mixed farming which brings stability to the agricultural industry.
The same cost of living increases have hit the Canadian people in every walk of life. We were faced with the same problem in dealing with veterans affairs. The soldier depending on a pension for his living finds that the $100 he gets today does not represent any more than the $50 he received 12 years ago. The old age pensioner is faced with the same difficulty. The Minister of Public Works finds that it costs him twice as much to build highways and carry out other construction today as it did a few years ago. The farmer is placed in a similar position because of exactly the same policy, and in order to save his industry he is demanding that it should be supported by means of floor prices or parity prices based on costs of production. If his prices are tied each year to his cost of production the farmer can continue to produce, and when he gets a crop he will be able to carry on.

I maintain that when the farmer is prosperous he buys wherever he can. He can pay his- taxes, electrify his farm and instal running water in his home. He likes to have a decent home in which to live, and he would like to have the amenities and modern standards of living that other Canadians enjoy. It is because farmers cannot have these things that young men leave the farms and go to industrial areas. This is not good for Canada. I am not going to repeat what I said the other night while the minister was here, except to point out what we believe is necessary in order for agriculture to take its place in the Canadian economy and make its contribution to the world through the feeding of hungry people.
Agriculture in Canada has a tremendous opportunity, and it is certainly very wrong for our farmers to be in the position that if they produce what they are able to produce they are left with surpluses on their hands that could be used to feed the hungry peoples of the earth. No person of good will would consider that there is too much food produced. We do not have enough food or enough people who know how to produce food to feed the hungry people of the world.
About a month ago the Minister of Defence Production told us that it would cost Canada approximately $122 million to put the first supersonic plane into production in about five years' time. About four times that amount is all that would be required to provide stability for Canadian agriculture so it could produce food to feed the hungry people of the world and win those people to the side of democracy who today are being won over to the side of communism. People from FAO and the United Nations will tell you that the democratic countries of the world have to have something more to show for democracy than bombs, guns and supersonic planes. If we can help to feed the needy and hungry of the world we will do more toward winning people to the side of democracy than will be achieved by the $2 billion we are spending on arms production, much of which will be completely obsolete by the time it gets into production in any quantity.
I leave these thoughts with the government on the first item, and I suggest that if they will extend floor prices into other fields of agriculture in line with the costs of production they will provide the necessary basis of stability for one of the greatest and most important industries of the country, an industry that can make a real contribution to democracy and place Canada high among the nations of the world.

Now that these estimates are before the house I want to make a few

casual observations, and I assure you I shall be very brief. Representing as I do an agricultural district, these estimates are of interest to me. In the last few years Canada has made tremendous progress in industrial development. Her pulp and paper industry has grown a great deal, as has the mining industry. Indeed, the over-all economy has expanded greatly. Industrial development may be of tremendous importance, but after all the basic industry is still agriculture. It is the mainspring of our prosperity. Unless we have a prosperous agriculture we will never have a sound economy in this country.
Within the last few years agriculture has been experiencing difficult times. I think 1952 was the all-time high in national income for agriculture. The year 1953 was fairly good, but not quite as good as 1952, and 1954 was a great deal lower than 1952 and considerably down from 1953. The first three months of 1955 have been down considerably from 1954.
I believe this points to a bad situation in agriculture. The cost of production has gone up and the national income of farmers has gone down. The cost of production probably will continue to go up, because mechanized farming has become a necessity today and agricultural implements have not come down in price but if anything have actually gone up a little. We must have more support.
We have heard a good deal in this house about western agriculture. Of course I appreciate that western agriculture is very important, but western agriculture has some advantages that eastern agriculture has not. If you will recall, the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act was passed, I think, in 1935.

This information came from the department, and they told me 1935. From 1935 to 1954 inclusive the amount paid to western agriculture under this act was practically $100 million. That was mainly spent in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan.
The Prairie Farm Assistance	Actperhaps I had better ask my friends when that was passed-came into effect in 1939. From 1939 to 1954 there has been approximately $200 million spent in prairie farm assistance, most of this coming from the federal treasury. I recall bringing this question up in the committee.
May I interrupt the hon. member? Can he tell us what the western farmers paid in tariffs over the same period?

Perhaps the hon. member will just keep quiet and let me finish this
Supply-Agriculture
speech; then he will have an opportunity. Perhaps after I am finished I will have an opportunity of answering some of his brilliant questions. I believe I asked this question in the committee on agriculture and I was told the federal department paid two-thirds and the shippers of grain paid one-third of the cost of this aid. We have no such insurance or protection in eastern Canada at all. Ontario really has had some very poor crops. If you will recall, last year in Ontario there were many acres of white beans that were never harvested at all. They were planted and some were pulled, while some were harvested and made into hog feed. The great bulk of them represented a loss. There were many hundreds of acres of sugar beets that were entirely lost because of weather which prevented harvesting. We had no way of being reimbursed. I would say that if the Prairie Farm Assistance Act is to continue across the board, we should take the word "prairie" out of it and make it the farm assistance act.
I do not want to start any discussions between eastern and western agriculture. I am quite anxious, and I think everybody is anxious, in the interests of the over-all economy of this country, that we should have a prosperous agriculture in both the east and the west. The western farmers had a good year in 1952. I think it was the best year they ever had. One of their own members put this on the record on April 22, and I was quite interested in it.
I called up the bureau of statistics to try to get the income taxes paid by farmers in Canada for 1953, but I have not a complete return yet. However, in 1952 there was approximately $27,454,000 paid by farmers across Canada. Of that amount there was some $13,268,000 paid by Saskatchewan farmers and $8,355,000 by Alberta farmers. They paid, therefore, a total of $21,518,000. It is difficult for me to believe, and I do not believe, that the income tax officials use a different yardstick in measuring income of the farmers from one end of this country to the other for tax purposes. They must have had a pretty good income in 1952, and I think again in 1953, although 1954 is probably a different story.
We have another problem that I think is quite serious as it affects the farmers in western Ontario. At the moment we are harvesting a crop of wheat. The Ontario crop amounts to approximately 25 million bushels. I can see our friends in the corner saying that is only a bagatelle, and I appreciate that it is only a bagatelle. They must agree, though, that to the farmers in this district 25 million bushels is a great deal. But not all

Supply-Agriculture
of that is sold as a cash crop. These last few years when the wheat was harvested, as it is being harvested now, the millers and the elevators undoubtedly took advantage of the situation. Storage was difficult to get and the farmers had to market the grain. Do you know that wheat that was being delivered at the start of this year was selling for $1.10 and $1.15 per bushel. Now it has been raised to $1.30 per bushel. Two months ago wheat was selling for $1.50 per bushel and now it is selling at $1.25, but the price of flour has not come down.
I think, therefore, the Ontario farmer must have some support to market his fall wheat. I would suggest to the Department of Agriculture that if this wheat cannot be directed through the wheat board, then the Agricultural Prices Support Act should be amended to put a floor price under Ontario wheat. I do not see how it can be handled any other way. I do not suppose it could be done under the marketing act because the marketing scheme has not operated yet. I do think the Ontario farmer is entitled to a little better protection. I do not see why the Agricultural Prices Support Act could not be amended to take care of it, because if I recall correctly the act states that it is to support the prices of agricultural products except wheat. Wheat is specifically exempted, so I think the act should be amended.
I am not going to take any more time, because there are some items on which I will probably want to speak as they come along. I do say, in the interests of agriculture across Canada, that we must have a bigger and better national farm income if we are going to be economically sound in this country.

Referring to item No. 2, Mr. Chairman, I presume that a speech made in the House of Commons by the Minister of Agriculture could be considered information and could come under the vote for information service. The minister said:
It Is the fact that these prices being kept in reasonable relationship to the prices of what farmers buy has resulted in the average net income of farmers being higher in the last four years than in any previous four-year period.
I suggest that it is proper to deal with this under the vote for the information service, Mr. Chairman. I have here a copy of the Economic Annalist for April, 1955. There may be a later edition, but the figures in this one are the same. I think the parliamentary assistant and members of the committee will agree that if we take the figures under the heading of farm prices of agricultural products, using this figure as the quotient of the figure when we take the period 1935-39 as 100; if we average the figures for those four years and compare them with the composite index of services used by farmers, and if we compare those two totals or the averages of those figures we would get the net income of farmers. And that is the only true income we have.
The average for those four years, 1951 to 1954, of the prices of agricultural products is 260-7, while the average of the prices farmers had to pay for commodities was 237-2, making a difference of 23-5. That is for the period 1951-54 inclusive.

I shall not be long. I just wish to refute this one thing, because it has been said so many times by the Minister of Agriculture and it is time somebody pointed out that it is not true. I know, and the farmers across Canada know, it is not true; but apparently a lot of people think it is true.
If one takes the figures for the four years 1947 to 1950 inclusive, as they appear in this booklet, he will find that the average price of farm products in those four years is 246-9, while the average price for commodities the farmer had to buy was 195-6, or a difference of 51-3. Surely this is evidence enough. The difference in the years 1951 to 1954 was 23-5 while in the period 1947 to 1950 inclusive it was 51-3. This means that the farmer's net income was represented by 51-3 in 1947-50 as against 23-5 in 1951-54.

Mr. Chairman, I find I have an apology to make to the hon. member for Lambton-Kent who spoke a moment ago, and who said the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act was passed in 1935. I interrupted him and said it was in 1934. I have checked and find I was in error. It was passed in 1935, in the last year of the Bennett government. I apologize to the hon. member.

Mr. Chairman, earlier this afternoon one hon. member on the other side of the chamber asked me if I were going to pose as an expert on agriculture. Very definitely I am not; but there are certain things that are obvious even to a city dweller like myself, that is provided he can read and provided he can figure.
One of these comes under the heading now before us. It is the unfortunate circumstance that the Department of Agriculture seems to have lost a couple of libraries, and I am worried about it. The situation is this, Mr. Chairman. The annual report of the national librarian for 1953 lists four libraries of the Department of Agriculture as having had their card catalogues microfilmed. There is the main departmental library, the botany division library, the central experimental farm library and the entomology division library.

But we find sessional paper 161-A, which was tabled on March 4, 1954, has the following question and answer:
How many individual libraries are maintained by government departments or agencies in Ottawa?
The answer from the Department of Agriculture is:
Two.
I have gone to the trouble of checking it up subsequently. There are four separate and distinct libraries in the Department of Agriculture. Perhaps this will serve as notice of that fact to the minister through his associate here in the house, and they can go out and track down these libraries and make sure they have them under their direction.
While I am on the subject of information services, Mr. Chairman, I do want to say that a good deal of work done under this classification and some of the publications for which this division is responsible would seem to me to be quite useful. I can see publications such as "The Gardener's Handbook"; "Herbaceous Perennials for Canadian Gardens"; I can even see "Ants and Their Control in Canada" and "Canadian Havens from Hay Fever"; but then we get into a slightly more indefinite area. I have some doubt about "Vitamin B12 for pregnant sows"; and there is another interesting publication, "Artificial Insemination of Turkeys" that may or may not have a wide distribution.
But the field on which I hesitate most to comment-I do not know whether or not the publication has been issued, but a great deal of work has been done by the department, I understand, in this field-is arsenic in hair. Apparently they analysed a good many samples of hair from residents of the Annapolis valley and discovered arsenic to be present in all samples, and that the concentration varied with the occupation. My purpose in mentioning this item is to suggest that the information section of the department be very careful before they issue another publication on arsenic in the hair of residents of the Annapolis valley to go along with the various others I have listed here this evening.

thing in the cherry industry of British Columbia. Because many plantings in the Okanagan valley are getting on in years the question of replanting is arising in a good many orchards, and the convention urged that research work be done in the propagation and planting of dwarf apple stock in order to find out whether any of the present marketable varieties are incompatible with certain root stocks, and to find the best stocks suited to the widely different soil conditions of the area. 5. Construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and new equipment, $1,676,995.

I am interested generally in this matter of science service, but as I read the items listed I think item 5 covers the area of particular interest. The science service branch of the department has been expanding its facilities very rapidly in recent years. That, of course, is as it should be because, dealing in fundamental research as it does, it is of basic importance to the agricultural industry.
Recently there was an announcement that a new science service laboratory is to be established on the University of Manitoba campus, I believe at a cost of $1 million. The latest information on that subject is to the effect that the laboratory will be in operation in January, 1957. The purpose behind

Supply-Agriculture
the establishment of this laboratory is, I understand, the general object of the science service branch, namely the consolidation of its pure research in one large laboratory, usually in association with a provincial university.
That raises one question in my mind which I would appreciate having answered this evening by the parliamentary assistant. Perhaps he would like to comment in a general way on the relationship between science service activities and the activities of the experimental farms branch. They overlap to a certain extent. In some respects they are complementary. I am a little hazy as to where they overlap and where they complement each other. I am particularly interested in learning what will be the activities originating in the new laboratory in Winnipeg with reference to field services.
Even fundamental pure research, of course, has as its final objective the assisting of the practical farmer in his practical farm situation. I raise this point because for the past 43 years the entomological laboratory for the province of Manitoba has been operating in the city of Brandon. It was established first of all by a gentleman, a naturalist of some capacities, named Norman Criddell and carried on under his direction until his death in 1933, when it moved to the new post office building in the city of Brandon.
Obviously the establishment of a new laboratory in the city of Winnipeg is going to mean a readjustment in the operation and functioning of the entomological laboratory in the city of Brandon. I would point out in that regard that its basic function has been to provide a field service to the farmers in the area. The city of Brandon is located in the centre of the Manitoba agricultural area. I have had some correspondence with the deputy minister on this matter, and I understand that under the new program the Brandon entomological activity will continue basically as a field service operation contacting the farmer at his place of operation.
However, one further problem arises, and here we come directly to the subject matter under item 5. There is a new public building in process in the city of Brandon, and the entomological department there has been expecting to occupy some space in this new building. I believe arrangements have gone sufficiently far that the space has all been allocated in the new building, and I understand that no provision is being made for the continuing activity of the entomological branch in the city of Brandon at their present offices in the post office building.

There is a certain degree of uncertainty because of the lack of information as to where their operations will be carried on in the future.
I would appreciate having a general comment on the division of activity between the new laboratory and the entomological activity in the city of Brandon. I would appreciate it also if the parliamentary assistant could briefly indicate the differences in function between the science service branch and the experimental farms branch and, finally, what provision will be made to house the Brandon field service operation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: In respect of the entomology branch that is now in the post office building in Brandon, it is the intention of the department to move it out to the experimental farm, which is right near the city. It is to do rush research work, which is very important in western Canada, and also to deal with regional problems in respect of rural matters in Manitoba.

I want to ask the parliamentary assistant about the new breed of hog that has been developed in Lacombe. I have not seen any announcement by the department about the new breed, but I have read about it in different newspapers. I have one article here from Country Life of June, 1955 which reads:
First Canadian breed of hogs ever produced, as announced from the Lacombe, Alberta experimental station, is more vigorous and faster growing, has a flatter back, floppy ears that almost cover the eyes and a fuller appearance with nice, round hams. When crossed with the Yorkshire, a bacon superior to that of Yorkshire is produced.
Then the article goes on to deal with the different characteristics. What I want to know is whether the Department of Agriculture is saying it is a better hog than the Yorkshire, or is it just something new? The article goes on to say:
Foundation of the new breed consists of ten Berkshire sows, five Landrace-Chester boars, which carried between 47 and 71 per cent Danish Land-race blood, and two pure Landrace boars. Average weaning weight of pigs is about 5 pounds greater than for Yorkshires. The latter have a slight advantage in average carcass score.
That means the Yorkshire is still the best hog when it goes on the rails.
Crossbreds of the two breeds appear to be equal or superior to either breed in all important economic traits.
Apparently this has all been accomplished in seven years. I have some other articles on the matter. It is stated that inbreeding had practically been done away with. It seems a very short time to have done away with inbreeding. I should like to have the parliamentary assistant give us some information. There is something else I have noticed in these reports. They emphasize the importance of the first cross. We know that the first cross is always good, and first crosses have won at Smithfield oftener than any pure breed ever did, but the trouble is that if you encourage this then the first thing that will happen is that we will have the farmers breeding crossbreds, and then we will have nothing but a bunch of mongrels again. We have a good pig in the Yorkshire. If the Department of Agriculture can produce something better I say good luck to them and I will give them every

credit for it. Have the department given out any information on the matter or is this just by the way?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The question asked by the hon. member for Selkirk is certainly important. He has a statement and so have I. I could read my statement to him, but I do not intend to do so tonight. However, those concerned feel that after seven careful years of breeding they have turned out a very good type of hog to cross with the Yorkshire, the Chester White and the Berkshire, but the best results are achieved by crossing with the Yorkshire. They have found that these crossbred pigs are equal or superior to other breeds in all important traits such as rate of gain and quality of the product.
As the hon. member has said, we have found over the years that the Yorkshire pig was probably the best type we could have for our purposes in Canada, and it has also been found to be the best type in the old land. Nevertheless we feel that if this hog is crossed with the Yorkshire the result will be a good bacon type of hog.
At the end of the seven years are these pigs free of black marks? Are they really white hogs?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture

I feel that the development of this new breed of livestock is quite an outstanding achievement of the animal husbandry branch of the Department of Agriculture, especially since it has been achieved in the very brief period of seven years. We hope the period of seven years has not been too brief and that the initial success will be continued in future years. Personally I should like to know when breeding stock of this new type of Lacombe hog will be available for distribution to Canadian farmers. When the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce were being considered I pointed out that during a hearing of a House of Commons committee on agriculture a letter was read by Mr. Milner indicating that a Department of Agriculture official had written to him regarding accusations made, or criticisms, with respect to feed screenings sent from the elevators at the head of the lakes. The official in the department, in answer to a letter written by Mr. Milner inquiring about the feeding value of wild buckwheat, which constituted 97 per cent of the feed screenings, said that wild buckwheat was a grain, and that its feeding value was not too different from that of ordinary grain. I do not know whether the actual analysis of wild buckwheat would compare favourably with barley or domestic buckwheat, but I would be interested to hear what the parliamentary assistant has to say. I do not believe it is proper to call wild buckwheat a grain.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Whether we should call wild buckwheat a grain is a matter of argument. Of course these screenings are a lot better than dirt. It is brought down from Fort William to eastern Canada. It will be a lot better than some of the dirt we find in these screenings. But whether it has the feed value of barley I am not in a position to say. However, we do know that our buckwheat in eastern Canada has good feed value.

That is domestic buckwheat, not wild buckwheat. Wild buckwheat is one of the worst weed seeds we have in the west or anywhere else, and to have it referred to as a grain is nonsense. I am not talking about the feed value of it, but referring to it only in connection with what was stated in the letter by this departmental official, where it was pointed out that its feed value was practically as good as, or very little below that of barley or domestic buckwheat. I am not sure whether domestic buckwheat was mentioned in the letter, but certainly the inference was that the feed value of wild buckwheat was practically as good as barley.

I have a copy of the Feeding Stuffs Act of the revised statutes of 1952. Regulation No. 1 under screening and scour-ings reads:
