speechtext: It is 1952.

No. 1 feed screenings-I have not the regulations with me-could contain, as I said, until this spring when it was changed, up to 97 per cent of cracked grain and wild buckwheat. Actually this is a proposal by the board of grain commissioners. The elevator operators themselves, knowing very well that they were doing wrong by sending this weed seed down to the feeders in Ontario, were willing to say that No. 1 feed screenings would have to contain at least 30 per cent cracked grain from now on; but until that time No. 1 feed screenings could contain 97 per cent wild buckwheat and cracked grain. If the assistant to the minister will check back on the regulations he will see that it could contain up to 97 per cent wild buckwheat and cracked grain, a combination of the two, so that it could actually contain 97 per cent of either one of them, or 97 per cent of wild buckwheat.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I am glad the hon. member has brought this to our attention. We shall certainly investigate to see whether what he says is true. These are the regulations under the Feeding Stuffs Act, 1952, in respect to 1955, the year of which we are now speaking. These are the regulations that are in effect today.

If these are new regulations then they must have been amended since that time. It may be a new printing of the regulations. I have not seen them until this time. As I say, until last spring it was true, and it was not good. The parliamentary assistant to the minister has not said anything about the fact that wild buckwheat may be described as grain.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: That may be a little difficult to answer. They are screenings for our purposes under these regulations. It is not a grain so far as we are concerned.

I have never before heard anyone refer to weed seed as a grain. There can be no doubt that wild buckwheat is one of the worst weeds we have. Why would it be referred to as grain? I suggest that the farmers out west are not paid for these weed seeds. They are not paid for weed seeds at all. It is dockage as far as they are concerned. The elevators at the head of the lakes clean it out of the grain and send it down to Ontario for feed. I do not know why anybody would pay the price for that kind of feed, but apparently some feeders do.

There are a number of farm marketing plans established under the Ontario farm products marketing act. A number of growers interested in the farm marketing legislation of Ontario have asked whether changes will be made in the marketing legislation. Commodity groups in Ontario are of the opinion that they cannot enact the legislation necessary for the effective marketing of farm products. Is this the opinion of the Department of Agriculture? As a supplementary question, is federal complementary legislation necessary?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
In respect to the question that is asked by the hon. member for Kent (Ont.), this is a very large question in the province of Ontario, and rightly so. I have prepared a short statement in respect to it, because I expected someone would ask this question tonight.
During the past few months the right of the provinces to legislate with respect to marketing boards has been questioned, and the province of Ontario has asked that legislation be passed by parliament giving the legislatures certain powers in this field. The Ontario legislation has not yet been held ultra vires, however, and it is also the case that certain legislation in other provinces providing for various kinds of marketing schemes has been upheld in the courts.
Under these circumstances the government decided that it would be unwise to attempt to deal with this problem without further discussion with the provincial governments and others who may be interested. Accordingly these discussions will be held before the next session, and we shall be in a better position to come to a decision as to the course to adopt.

Certainly in cases like this the opposition is bearing the burden of the whole session. All the government has to do is sit in their seats. The opposition has to bear the burden. You would not agree to it.

If unanimous consent means anything, let us have it. If it does not, let us forget it. I very much object to going over ten o'clock. Those of us who attend to the business of the house begin at eleven o'clock in the morning and go until ten at night.
Those of us who are on farms, when we go back, will be working more than a 7^-hour day. So far as I am concerned I am willing to go on longer.

I am willing to go on longer if we pass a regulation that it is to be 10.30. We should abide by the regulation. We should not pass a resolution that we are going to stop at ten o'clock and then slide over to any period after ten. There is no logic in that.
